question: M1
answer:
BASICMED (US) — AIRCRAFT LIMITS: MAXIMUM TAKEOFF WEIGHT, AUTHORIZED OCCUPANTS, PASSENGERS ON BOARD

Regulatory basis: 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) as amended by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63, Sec. 828, 'Expansion of BasicMed'), effective for operations on or after 12 November 2024. Current FAA guidance reflecting the amendment: Notice N 8000.386 (dated 11/14/24); FAA newsroom release 15 Nov 2024; FAA BasicMed program page.

1. ANSWER (current law, on/after 12 Nov 2024)

  (a) Maximum takeoff weight .......... 12,500 lb — maximum CERTIFICATED takeoff weight (MTOW), not actual weight.
  (b) Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry .......... 7 occupants (including the pilot in command and any required flightcrew).
  (c) Passengers on board .......... 6 passengers.

  Source text: 'Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board.' (N 8000.386, para. a.(2)).
  Corroboration: 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants / Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds ... Carries not more than six passengers' (FAA BasicMed page). 'Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.' (FAA newsroom, 15 Nov 2024).

2. SUPERSEDED VALUES — do not use for current operations

  Pre-12 Nov 2024 BasicMed (still printed in AC 68-1A, 5/3/17, and the Jul/Aug 2017 FAA Safety Briefing): 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight; not more than 6 occupants authorized; not more than 5 passengers. AC 68-1A has not been reissued to reflect PL 118-63 and is therefore stale on these three numbers; it remains usable for its definitions and interpretive material (design-approval mechanics, experimental aircraft, occupant counting). Any answer citing 6,000 / 6 / 5 as the current limits is out of date.

3. HOW EACH LIMIT IS MEASURED (the operative distinctions)

  3.1 Maximum takeoff weight — 'maximum certificated takeoff weight' is a product of the aircraft's certification, not a number the pilot can manage downward. You may not fly a heavier-certificated aircraft under BasicMed by loading less fuel or payload to stay under 12,500 lb. For type-certificated aircraft it appears on the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) / design approval; for experimental aircraft it is the maximum gross weight established by the operator and accepted by the FAA in the operating limitations issued with the Special Airworthiness Certificate (AC 68-1A 5.1.3).

  3.2 Authorized occupants — the count the aircraft is AUTHORIZED to carry under its design approval (TC, STC, or amended TC) or, for experimental aircraft, its operating limitations — not the number of seats actually installed. An aircraft certificated for 8 occupants does not become a covered aircraft by removing a seat; a new design approval (STC/ATC) is required. Example from FAA guidance: variants of the Piper PA-32/PA-34 certificated to more than 6 occupants did not qualify under the original rule even with only 6 seats installed, and AOPA obtained an STC permitting BasicMed operation of PA-32 models once the optional 7th seat is removed — the STC, not the seat removal alone, is what changes the authorization. Occupants include the PIC and any required pilot flightcrew.

  3.3 Passengers on board — an operational limit on the flight, distinct from the authorization limit. Passengers = occupants minus the PIC and minus any other required flightcrew. Worked examples under the current 7-occupant / 6-passenger rule:
     - Aircraft certificated for one pilot: PIC + up to 6 passengers = 7 occupants. Compliant.
     - Aircraft certificated for two pilots (or where the regulations require two): PIC + required second pilot + up to 5 passengers = 7 occupants. Compliant.
     - A training flight carrying a flight instructor counts the instructor as an occupant; the instructor may be a passenger, a required flightcrew member, or an additional crew member depending on the operation, but in every case the arithmetic must not exceed 7 occupants and 6 passengers.
     - 8 occupants (e.g., 2 crew + 6 passengers) is NOT compliant even though passengers alone are 6: the authorization limit is exceeded.

4. TWO AIRCRAFT-SPECIFIC QUALIFICATIONS

  4.1 Transport category helicopters. The statutory expansion of the weight limit to 12,500 lb excludes transport category helicopters. Treat the weight increase as NOT available to transport category helicopters; the prior 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight continues to govern them pending issuance of updated FAA advisory material. The occupant limit (7) and passenger limit (6) are not affected by that exclusion.

  4.2 Experimental aircraft. 14 CFR 91.319(j) historically barred carrying more than six occupants in an experimental aircraft under BasicMed. That text predates PL 118-63 and it should not be assumed, without checking the current regulation text, that it was conformed upward to seven. For experimental aircraft, verify the current 91.319(j) text and the aircraft's own operating limitations before relying on a 7-occupant authorization; the MTOW is taken from the operating limitations. This qualification does not change the three headline figures for aircraft generally.

5. RELATED BASICMED LIMITS (context only — not the three asks)

  Flight must be conducted at or below 18,000 ft MSL; within the United States or another country in which BasicMed is authorized; at an indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots; not for compensation or hire. (Note: the 250-knot limit is an operating limit on the flight, not an aircraft-certification limit — a 300-knot-capable aircraft may still be a covered aircraft if it meets the weight and occupant limits and is flown within them.)

6. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST FOR A GIVEN AIRCRAFT

  Step 1 — Confirm the operation is on/after 12 Nov 2024 (otherwise use 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers).
  Step 2 — Read the certificated MTOW from the TCDS/design approval (or experimental operating limitations). Require <= 12,500 lb (<= 6,000 lb if a transport category helicopter).
  Step 3 — Read the authorized occupant count from the same design approval (or operating limitations). Require <= 7. Do not substitute installed seat count.
  Step 4 — For the planned flight, count bodies: total occupants <= 7 AND passengers (occupants minus PIC and required flightcrew) <= 6.
  Step 5 — Confirm the flight also satisfies 18,000 ft, airspeed 250 KIAS, geographic, and no-compensation limits.
  Step 6 — Record the source and date relied on; the figures above are current as of the FAA guidance dated 14–15 November 2024 and should be re-verified against the current 14 CFR 61.113(i) text and the current edition of AC 68-1 before being relied on for a specific operation.

7. SCOPE NOTE

  This states the US BasicMed aircraft limits under the FAA regime current at the date of the cited guidance. It is a compliance summary of regulatory limits, not a legal opinion or a determination for any specific aircraft or flight; foreign operations depend on the authorizing state's acceptance of BasicMed.

question: M3
answer:
# Hours of Service — Passenger-Carrying CMV (Motorcoach), US Federal

## Rule set applied
49 CFR Part 395, **§ 395.5 (Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles)** — the passenger-carrier rule set, which is deliberately different from the property-carrier rule set in § 395.3. Scope assumed (and fixed by the request itself): a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle operating in interstate commerce in the United States, with no exemption claimed. Definitions of driving/on-duty/off-duty are those of § 395.2.

## Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may they drive? | **10 hours** | § 395.5(a)(1) — “More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty” is prohibited |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty may they drive? | **8 consecutive hours** | § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) — both limits run “following 8 consecutive hours off duty” |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours** | § 395.5(a)(2) — no driving “for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty” |

Source text relied on (FMCSA, *Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers*, FMCSA-E-06-006, July 2022, and the FMCSA “Hours of Service – Motor Carriers of Passengers” web page, both quoting § 395.5):

> “No motor carrier of passengers shall permit or require any passenger-carrying CMV driver to drive: • More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, or • For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.”

## How the three limits interact (the part that is usually gotten wrong)

These are **two independent caps plus one reset**, and the driver must satisfy all of them simultaneously:

1. **Reset condition (ask 2).** No driving at all until 8 consecutive hours off duty have been completed. The 8 hours must be *consecutive* off-duty time; it is the anchor for both caps.
2. **Driving cap (ask 1).** Within a duty period, total driving time may not exceed 10 hours.
3. **On-duty cap (ask 3).** Driving must stop at the 15th hour after the driver came on duty following the 8-hour reset — **regardless of how much driving time remains**. A driver who has driven only 6 hours but has been on duty 15 hours may not drive further. Conversely, a driver who reaches 10 hours of driving at hour 12 of the duty period may not drive further even though 3 hours of the 15-hour window remain.

Worked example (single duty period, 8-hour reset completed at 06:00):

- On duty 06:00 → the 15-hour on-duty cap expires at **21:00**. No driving at or after 21:00.
- If the driver begins driving at 06:00, the 10-hour driving cap is reached at **16:00**; driving must end by 16:00 unless earlier stops/interruptions push it later — but in no case later than 21:00.
- If dispatching inserts 5 hours of non-driving on-duty work first (06:00–11:00), driving may run 11:00–21:00, i.e. the driver is capped at **10 hours of driving ending exactly at the 21:00 on-duty limit**; the two caps bind at the same instant.
- Either way, the driver may not drive again until 8 more consecutive hours off duty are complete.

## What this rule set does *not* contain (avoid transplanting property-carrier numbers)

For passenger-carrying CMVs there is **no 11-hour driving limit, no 14-hour on-duty window, and no 30-minute break requirement** — those are property-carrier provisions (§ 395.3). Using 11/14/30 for a motorcoach is the most common error in this area.

## Secondary limits and provisions worth stating alongside the three answers

- **Weekly cumulative on-duty cap (§ 395.5(b))** — separate from, and additional to, the 15-hour daily cap: **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days** if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week, or **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days** if it does. This is a cumulative on-duty total, not a driving total, and it is *not* the answer to ask 3; ask 3 is the 15-hour duty-period limit. Which of 60/70 applies depends on the carrier's operating schedule, which the request does not specify, so both are stated.
- **Sleeper berth (§ 395.1(g)(3))** — a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth (as defined in § 393.76) may accumulate the equivalent of the 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. So “8 consecutive hours” may be satisfied in split form only through that specific provision; absent it, the 8 hours must be genuinely consecutive.
- **Short-haul / record-of-duty-status exception (§ 395.1(e))** — a driver operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released from duty within 14 consecutive hours is exempt from the logbook/RODS requirement; § 395.1(e)(1)(iii)(B) requires such a passenger-carrying driver to have at least **8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty**. This 14-hour figure is an *exception-eligibility condition* and is **stricter** than, and does not replace, the 15-hour limit in § 395.5(a)(2). A driver claiming this exception is effectively held to 14 hours; a driver not claiming it is held to 15. The three answers above are the baseline rule.
- **Travel/relief-driver time (§ 395.1(j))** — travel to a layover location at the carrier's direction (“cushioning”) counts as on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case the entire travel period is off duty. Relief-driver travel: if driven or using public transportation, and 8 consecutive hours off duty follow arrival, the travel may be recorded as off duty; if the driver drives himself/herself in a non-CMV, that time is on duty (not driving).
- **Recordkeeping** — non-business private motor carriers of passengers are exempt from the RODS/ELD recordkeeping requirements of Part 395, but the § 395.5 driving and on-duty limits still apply to their drivers; the exemption is evidentiary, not substantive.

## Exceptions that can lawfully extend the limits (verify before relying)

- **Adverse driving conditions (§ 395.1(b))** — may permit additional driving to complete the run. The precise scope and any hour extension applicable to passenger-carrying drivers was not present in the source material reviewed for this answer and must be read from the current § 395.1(b) text before being applied; it is situational and does not change the baseline 10/8/15 above.
- **Emergency relief (§ 390.23)** — declared emergencies suspend Parts 390–399 for the duration of the relief period; situational and declaration-dependent.
- **State intrastate rules** — a driver never crossing a state line, or operating wholly intrastate in a state with its own passenger HOS rules, may be governed by different numbers. The answers above are the federal interstate rule set, which the request’s framing (“in the US”, motorcoach) invokes.

## Verification

Check the three figures directly against the current eCFR text of **49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2)**, and cross-check against FMCSA’s passenger-carrier HOS publication (FMCSA-E-06-006). Both sources reviewed for this answer state 10 hours driving, 8 consecutive hours off duty, 15 hours on duty, and the figures are unchanged across the 2023, 2024 and 2025 CFR volumes reviewed. If the operation is intrastate-only, or an exception in the list above is being claimed, re-derive before publishing these numbers to drivers.

question: M5
answer:
Compliance answer — 14 CFR Part 135 flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less.

1. Applicability. Section 135.273 applies to flight attendants in all operations conducted under Part 135 (see §135.261(e)). An on-demand charter operator does not avoid §135.273 merely because the operation is on-demand rather than scheduled passenger-carrying. The rule applies when a flight attendant is assigned as a flight attendant; if no flight attendant is required or assigned, there is no §135.273 rest obligation for a flight attendant.

2. Baseline rest — ask 1. Under §135.273(b)(2), a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less under §135.273(b)(1) must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. The rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. The 14-hour threshold includes exactly 14 hours. For this ask, the required rest is 9 consecutive hours.

3. Permitted reduction — ask 2. Under §135.273(b)(3), the 9-hour rest period required by §135.273(b)(2) may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. That subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period, and it must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. The reduction is therefore conditional, not automatic: the operator must be able to schedule the 10-hour subsequent rest within the 24-hour window.

4. Operational constraints. Section 135.273(b)(10) prohibits assigning a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section. Section 135.273(b)(11) prohibits assigning a flight attendant to perform any duty during a required rest period. Section 135.273(b)(13) separately requires at least 24 consecutive hours free from all further duty during any 7 consecutive calendar days. Rest period is defined in §135.273(a) as the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise. Under §135.273(b)(14), a flight attendant is not considered scheduled for duty in excess of the duty period limitations if the flights were scheduled and normally terminate within the limitations but, due to circumstances beyond the certificate holder's control such as adverse weather, are not at departure expected to reach destination within the scheduled time.

5. Scheduling example. If the scheduled duty period ends at 22:00, the baseline 9-hour rest permits the next duty period to begin no earlier than 07:00 the following day. If the operator uses the 8-hour reduction, rest may run 22:00–06:00, but the operator must also schedule a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 22:00 the following day (24 hours after the 22:00 start of the reduced rest) and occurring between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. In practice, the duty period following the reduced rest must end early enough that the 10-hour subsequent rest can begin by that 22:00 deadline.

6. Caveats. This answer states the federal regulatory minimum under the default §135.273(b) flight-attendant rules. It assumes no §135.273(c) election to apply the flight crewmember flight time and duty rules to flight attendants; if the certificate holder has made that election in its written procedures, the applicable rest matrix is different and must be checked against the election and the operator's manual. It also assumes no exemption, deviation, operations specification, or collective bargaining agreement imposes a different rule. An operator manual, OPSPEC, or labor agreement may be stricter than 9 hours and may restrict or prohibit the 8-hour reduction; the operator must comply with the most restrictive applicable requirement. Duty periods above 14 hours have separate rest requirements under §135.273(b)(4)–(b)(9) and are outside this question.

Bottom line: baseline rest = 9 consecutive hours; reducible to 8 consecutive hours only with a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest and occurring between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

question: M7
answer:
ANSWER

1) Current specification of HTTP/2: **RFC 9113**, "HTTP/2", M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla) and C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.), June 2022, Standards Track (maturity level: Proposed Standard).

2) RFC 9113 obsoletes exactly two RFCs:
   - **RFC 7540** — "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", Belshe/Peon/Thomson, May 2015 (the original HTTP/2 core specification).
   - **RFC 8740** — "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", D. Benjamin, February 2020 (which had *updated* RFC 7540; RFC 9113 folds its content in and obsoletes it).

So the obsolete set is {RFC 7540, RFC 8740} — two documents. Answering "RFC 7540" alone is incomplete.

EVIDENCE (verbatim from authoritative RFC metadata)

- RFC 9113 header block, rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html:
  "RFC: 9113 / Obsoletes: 7540, 8740 / Category: Standards Track / Published: June 2022 / ISSN: 2070-1721"
- RFC 9113, Section 1 (Introduction):
  "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740. Appendix B lists notable changes."
- RFC 9113, Appendix B (Changes from RFC 7540):
  "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."
- RFC 7540 info page, rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/:
  "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113. This RFC was updated, see RFC 8740."
- RFC 8740 header block, rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8740.html:
  "RFC: 8740 / Updates: 7540 / Published: February 2020" — i.e. 8740 was an *update* to 7540 and is now itself obsoleted by 9113.
- No "Obsoleted by" entry exists for RFC 9113 in the RFC Editor / datatracker metadata as of the fetch (2026-11-17), which is what makes 9113 the *current* HTTP/2 specification rather than a superseded one.

SCOPE BOUNDARIES (what is deliberately NOT in the answer)

- **Updates ≠ Obsoletes.** RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2) carries "Updates: 7540"; it is not obsoleted by RFC 9113 and is not listed in 9113's Obsoletes header. It remains an active extension. Only the Obsoletes header defines the answer to ask 2.
- **RFC 7541 (HPACK)** is referenced by, not obsoleted by, RFC 9113. HPACK remains the current header-compression spec for HTTP/2.
- **HTTP semantics** come from RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics); RFC 9113 specifies the HTTP/2 wire protocol/transport binding only. RFC 9113 is the answer to "HTTP/2 specification", not RFC 9110.
- **HTTP/3 (RFC 9114)** is out of scope; the ask is HTTP/2.
- **Errata** do not alter the Obsoletes header; no erratum changes the set {7540, 8740}.

VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (reproducible, no tooling required)

1. Fetch https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ and read the metadata block: confirm "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740" and the absence of an "Obsoleted by" / "Updated by" banner. Absence of an obsoleting document is the test for "current".
2. Cross-check the body: RFC 9113 Section 1 must contain "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." This guards against a metadata-only transcription error.
3. Cross-check the reverse direction: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/ must say "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113." and https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8740/ must show it as obsoleted by 9113. A one-directional match indicates a stale mirror; trust the pair only when both directions agree.
4. Optional machine check: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ — the "Obsoletes" field must read 7540, 8740, and "Obsoleted by" must be empty.
5. If step 1 later shows an "Obsoleted by" entry, the answer changes: replace RFC 9113 with that document and re-read *its* Obsoletes header (an obsoleting document need not itself list 7540/8740 if the chain is indirect — in that case report the immediate obsoleter and note the transitive chain).

One-line result: current HTTP/2 spec = RFC 9113 (June 2022); it obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.

The first reads: "Information about the current status of this document, any errata, and how to provide feedback on it may be obtained at http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540."

question: M9
answer:
UK STATUTORY MINIMUM WAGE RATES FROM 1 APRIL 2026 — ANSWER AND BRIEFING NOTE

1. THE TWO FIGURES ASKED FOR

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Preceding rate (to 31 Mar 2026) | Increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over) | £12.71 per hour | £12.21 | +£0.50 (+4.1%) |
| National Minimum Wage, 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 per hour | £10.00 | +£0.85 (+8.5%) |

Effective date: 1 April 2026. The rates apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after that date; a pay period straddling 1 April must be apportioned or the new rate applied from the first full period, per the employer's normal practice, but the statutary liability is the new rate for hours worked from 1 April 2026 onwards.

These are gross hourly rates before tax, NICs and pension deductions.

2. CONFIRMATION STATUS (the key correctness risk, addressed)

The figures are not merely Low Pay Commission (LPC) recommendations — they are confirmed, Government-accepted, and legislated:

- Statutory Instrument: The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, No. 357, laid in draft before Parliament under s.51(5) National Minimum Wage Act 1998 and approved by resolution of each House. Reg 1(2): comes into force 1 April 2026. Reg 1(3): extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Reg 2(2) substitutes "£12.71" for "£12.21" in reg 4 of the 2015 Regulations (the National Living Wage). Reg 2(3)(a) substitutes "£10.85" for "£10.00" in reg 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21).
- GOV.UK statutary rates page ('National Minimum Wage rates'): April 2026 row gives 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85.
- GOV.UK 'Minimum wage rates for 2026' (LPC, published 26 November 2025): states 'The Government has announced the 2026 increases... The Government accepted in full the recommendations of the independent Low Pay Commission.' Table: NLW £12.71, 18-20 rate £10.85.
- LPC 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (published 1 April 2026): same table, and states the new rates come into force on 1 April 2026.

So the answer is safe to use for payroll, costing and contract purposes for hours worked from 1 April 2026.

3. THE REST OF THE APRIL 2026 TABLE (included because a rate change is rarely used in isolation)

| Band | From 1 April 2026 |
|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 |
| Accommodation offset (max per day) | £11.10 |

Apprentice rate applies where the worker is under 19, or is 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 19+ who has completed the first year moves to the full rate for their age (e.g. £12.71 if 21+).

4. SCOPE, EXCLUSIONS AND CAVEATS AN HR FUNCTION SHOULD FLAG

- This is the statutary National Living Wage, not the voluntery 'Real Living Wage' published by the Living Wage Foundation (a separate, higher, non-statutary figure with its own annual date and London weighting). Do not mix the two in pay polices or adverts.
- Age is determined by the worker's age on the last day of the pay reference period, not on the first day.
- The 21+ threshold reflects the band structure in force since 1 April 2024 (previously 23+ from April 2021, and 25+ before that). Pre-April-2024 comparisions in long-run data need that break noted.
- Rates are UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland); minimum wage is not devolved, so there is no Scottish/Welsh/NI variation to apply.
- Accomodation offset rises to £11.10 per day: where an employer provides living accomodation, the offset reduces the wages which count for minimum wage purposes and must be recalculated.
- Salary sacrifice, benefits in kind, unpad working time, travel time between assignments, uniform/safety equipment deductions and tip treatment all affect compliance calcuations; a headline rate change is the trigger to re-run those checks, not a substitute for them.
- Enforsement and penalties sit with HMRC (including the naming scheme and the 200% arrears penalty up to £20,000 per worker); rate changes are a common source of accidental underpayment in the first pay run of April.

5. ACTIONS FOR THE APRIL 2026 UPLIFT (practical checklist)

1. Update payroll rate tables effective 1 April 2026: £12.71 / £10.85 / £8.00 / £8.00; accomodation offset £11.10/day.
2. Re-run an age-band audit against date of birth so no 21st birthday and no 18th birthday falls into the wrong band in April.
3. Re-check salaried staff whose contracted hours imply an hourly rate below £12.71 — overtimed salaried roles are the most common breach.
4. Recalculate any accomodation-offset arrangements at £11.10.
5. Update offer letters, contracts and recruiter adverts that quote hourly rates; remove references to £12.21/£10.00.
6. Diarise a re-check for the April 2027 rates (already published as indicative: £13.21 / £11.27 / £8.31 / £8.31) and for the next LPC recommendation cycle in autumn 2026.

6. SOURCES AND VALIDITY WINDOW

- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (draft SI 2026 No. 357), legislation.gov.uk.
- GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage rates' (statutary rates page).
- GOV.UK / Low Pay Commission, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026', published 26 November 2025.
- GOV.UK / Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', published 1 April 2026.
Validity: these rates hold for pay periods from 1 April 2026 until supplanted on 1 April 2027.

question: M11
answer:
ANSWER — FMCSA short-haul exception to the record-of-duty-status requirement, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)

1) RADIUS: The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation parenthetically converts this to 172.6 statute miles. Air miles are straight-line (great-circle) miles, not highway miles — a driver may legally drive more than 172.6 road miles and still be inside a 150 air-mile circle.

2) RELEASE FROM WORK: The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The 14 hours run from the time the driver comes on duty; they are elapsed clock hours, not cumulative on-duty hours.

OPERATIVE REGULATORY TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), current eCFR):

"(e) Short-haul operations —
(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing:
(A) The time the driver reports for duty each day;
(B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day;
(C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and
(D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

WHAT COUNTS AS THE 'NORMAL WORK REPORTING LOCATION':
Part 395 does not carry a standalone definition of the term in § 395.2. The regulation supplies its own gloss in § 395.1(e)(2)(ii): 'the location where the driver reports to and is released from work, i.e., the normal work reporting location.' Practically, it is the single fixed terminal/yard/facility where the driver signs in at the start of the duty tour and is released at the end. Because (e)(1)(ii) requires return to that location, a driver whose tour ends anywhere other than the reporting location does not qualify for that day, even if inside the radius.

FULL QUALIFICATION CHECKLIST (all must hold; failure of any one voids the exception for that day):
1. Operates within 150 air miles of the normal work reporting location.
2. Returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours of coming on duty.
3. Not a driver-salesperson (driver-salespersons are excluded from (e)(1)(ii) relief and cannot use this branch).
4. Property-carrying: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty. Passenger-carrying: at least 8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
5. Carrier keeps and retains for 6 months accurate time records of report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and (for new/intermittent drivers) the preceding 7 days per § 395.8(j)(2).
6. The 11-hour driving limit and the 60/70-hour limits of § 395.3 are unaffected by the exception — the exception relieves only the RODS requirement of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 (and, for property carriers, the 30-minute break).

PROPERTY vs PASSENGER: The two figures asked about are identical in both contexts — 150 air miles and 14 consecutive hours. The only property/passenger divergence inside (e)(1) is the off-duty interval (10 hours property, 8 hours passenger). So the property/passenger ambiguity does not change either answer.

NON-CDL VARIANT, § 395.1(e)(2) (flagged so the numbers are not misread):
A second short-haul branch applies to property-carrying CMVs that do not require a CDL. It uses the same 150 air-mile radius ('within a 150 air-mile radius of the location where the driver reports to and is released from work, i.e., the normal work reporting location'), requires return to that location at the end of each duty tour, and permits driving — not release — after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7. For the question as asked (release from work under the RODS-relieving short-haul exception), the controlling figure is 14 consecutive hours; the 16-hour allowance is a driving-window allowance on two days per week, not a general release time, and does not convert the answer to 16.

HISTORICAL NOTE (superseded — do not apply):
Before the 2020 HOS final rule (FMCSA, 'Hours of Service of Drivers,' RIN 2126-AC19; NPRM published August 2019; final rule effective September 29, 2020), the short-haul exception read 100 air miles (115.08 statute miles) and a 12-hour duty period. FMCSA's own summary of the change: 'change the short-haul exception ... by lengthening the drivers' maximum on-duty period from 12 to 14 hours and extending the distance limit within which the driver may operate from 100 air miles to 150 air miles.' Any document, logbook form, or carrier policy still reciting 100 air miles / 12 hours is out of date.

CONSEQUENCE OF EXCEEDING EITHER LIMIT:
If the driver leaves the 150 air-mile radius or is not released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception does not apply for that day and the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day. Per FMCSA's Driver's Guide to Hours of Service: 'If the individual cannot meet the terms of the exception (e.g., the driver goes beyond the distance limitation or works too many hours), the driver must complete a RODS for that day as soon as' practicable. The time-record requirement is not a substitute for RODS on a non-qualifying day.

ONE-LINE ANSWER:
150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) and 14 consecutive hours.

# Hours of Service for Drivers of Passenger-Carrying CMVs (US Federal, FMCSA)

**Scope of this answer.** Driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle (motorcoach/bus) operating in interstate commerce under US federal rules, 49 CFR Part 395, Subpart B. Governing provision: **49 CFR 395.5** ("Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles"), issued at 70 FR 50073 (Aug. 25, 2005) and reproduced unchanged in the current eCFR and in the 2025 printed CFR (Title 49, Vol. 5). No state variation, no short-haul exception, no adverse conditions assumed for the three headline figures.

---

## 1. The three answers

| # | Question | Answer | Regulation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may they drive? | **10 hours** | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** | 49 CFR 395.5(a) (opening clause governing both (a)(1) and (a)(2)) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours on duty** | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2) |

### Operative regulatory text (49 CFR 395.5(a))

> "Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:
>
> (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
>
> (1) More than **10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty**; or
>
> (2) For any period after having been **on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty**."

Read the sentence structure precisely, because it is where most misstatements originate:

- The **8 consecutive hours off duty** is a single precondition that attaches to *both* limits. It is not a separate "8-hour driving window," and it is not an 8-hour cap on anything. It is the daily reset.
- The **10 hours** is a *cumulative* driving cap within the tour of duty — it is not a limit on continuous driving. The FMCSA guide is explicit: "There is no limit on how many of those hours you are allowed to drive at one time — you may drive for as little as a few minutes or as much as 10 hours in a row." A driver may drive 3 hours, go off duty, drive 7 more, and be at the cap.
- The **15 hours** is the on-duty threshold, measured from coming on duty following the 8-hour reset. After 15 on-duty hours the driver may continue to perform non-driving work but **may not drive**. Off-duty time taken during the day does **not** extend the 15-hour period (unlike the property-carrier 14-hour rule, which is a consecutive clock; the passenger 15-hour rule excludes off-duty time from the count).

### Verification arithmetic

- 10 driving hours must be consumed **inside** the 15 on-duty hours: 10 < 15 ✓. A driver who drives the full 10 has at most 5 on-duty, non-driving hours remaining, and may not drive past the 15th on-duty hour regardless of how much of the 10-hour driving allowance remains.
- Both clocks are re-armed only by **8 consecutive hours off duty**. Off-duty or sleeper-berth time shorter than 8 consecutive hours (e.g., a lunch break) resets neither the 10-hour driving count nor the 15-hour on-duty count.
- Worked example (from FMCSA's Interstate Passenger-Carrying Driver's Guide): 8 continuous hours off; on duty at 06:00; work 7 hours; 1 hour off for lunch; work 8 more hours until 22:00. Total on-duty = 15 hours (the lunch hour does not count). The driver **must not drive after 22:00** but may perform other work. No further driving until another 8 consecutive hours off duty.

---

## 2. Secondary limit that also bars driving — the 60/70-hour rule

49 CFR 395.5(b) independently prohibits driving once the weekly on-duty accumulator is reached, regardless of how many motor carriers the driver serves:

| Carrier operates CMVs… | Limit | Window |
|---|---|---|
| Not every day of the week | **60 hours on duty** | any 7 consecutive days |
| Every day of the week | **70 hours on duty** | any 8 consecutive days |

Key points:

- **All on-duty time counts**, including work for other motor carriers and compensated work for non-motor carriers. The FMCSA Safety Planner states: "If a driver of a passenger-carrying vehicle works more than one job of any kind, that time must also be included as on-duty time." Multiple-employer drivers must furnish a signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty (§ 395.8(j)).
- **There is no 34-hour restart in the passenger-carrier rule.** The 34-hour restart provision sits in the property-carrier section (§ 395.3(c)); § 395.5(b) contains no such provision, and the FMCSA passenger guide describes the reset as follows: "Once you reach the 60-hour limit, you will not be able to drive again until you have dropped below 60 hours for a 7-consecutive-day period." Do not advise a motorcoach driver that a 34-hour reset reopens the weekly clock under § 395.5.

---

## 3. Exceptions that change the numbers (apply only if their conditions are met)

These are stated so the base answers above are not misapplied; the headline values remain 10 / 8 / 15.

### 3.1 Adverse driving conditions — § 395.1(b)

| Limit | Base | Maximum with adverse conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Driving after 8 consecutive hours off duty | 10 h | **12 h** (+2) |
| On duty after 8 consecutive hours off duty | 15 h | **17 h** (+2) |

Applies only to conditions at the time of driving that the driver could not reasonably know about before starting (snow, ice, fog, unusual traffic congestion). It is not a discretionary buffer. 12 < 17, so the internal ordering of the two limits is preserved.

### 3.2 Sleeper berth — § 395.1(g)(3)

A driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth (as defined in § 393.76) may accumulate the equivalent of the 8 consecutive off-duty hours by taking **two rest periods in the sleeper berth**, provided all four requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. Per FMCSA: the driver "must take at least 8 hours in the sleeper berth, and may split the sleeper berth time into two periods provided neither is less than 2 hours. All sleeper berth pairings MUST add up to at least 8 hours." **This is materially different from the property-carrier split (2 h + 7 h = 10 h)** — the property-carrier 2/7 pairing and 10-hour total do not apply to passenger carriers.

### 3.3 Short-haul exception — § 395.1(e)

A driver is exempt from the record-of-duty-status requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if the driver operates **within a 150 air-mile radius** of the normal work reporting location and **does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours** (report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours). This is a *paperwork* relief; it does not enlarge the 10-hour driving cap or the 15-hour on-duty threshold.

### 3.4 Travel / relief-driver time — § 395.1(j)

Time spent traveling at the carrier's direction but not driving ("cushioning") counts as **on duty** unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case the entire period is off duty. A relief driver driven or using public transportation to a layover who then gets 8 consecutive hours off duty may record the travel as off duty; a driver who drives him/herself in a non-CMV to the layover must record that time as **on duty, not driving** (it consumes the 15-hour window without consuming the 10-hour driving allowance).

---

## 4. What does *not* apply to passenger carriers (common error list)

| Property-carrier rule | Passenger-carrier rule |
|---|---|
| 11-hour driving limit | **10-hour** driving limit |
| 10 consecutive hours off duty | **8 consecutive** hours off duty |
| 14-hour consecutive driving window (off-duty does not extend) | **15-hour** on-duty limit (off-duty time is not counted toward it) |
| 30-minute break after 8 cumulative driving hours | **No 30-minute break requirement** |
| 34-hour restart of the 60/70 clock | **No restart provision in § 395.5(b)** |
| Split sleeper: 2 h + 7 h = 10 h | Split sleeper: two periods, neither < 2 h, totaling **8 h** |

---

## 5. Compliance notes (context, not part of the three values)

- **Record of duty status.** Passenger-carrier drivers are generally subject to § 395.8 RODS; non-business private motor carriers of passengers are not subject to the Part 395 recordkeeping requirements. Drivers qualifying for § 395.1(e) short-haul relief are exempt from §§ 395.8 and 395.11.
- **ELD.** ELD rules apply to most motor carriers of passengers and their drivers who are required to keep a RODS, including drivers domiciled in Canada and Mexico operating in the US absent an exception. Exception example: drivers required to prepare a RODS no more than 8 days in any 30-day period.
- **Retention.** RODS and supporting documents must be retained not less than 6 months (§ 395.8(k)).
- **Multi-carrier duty.** § 395.5(b) applies "regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services."

---

## 6. Sources

1. 49 CFR 395.5 — https://ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.5
2. FMCSA, *Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers* — https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/safety/carrier-safety/hours-service-motor-carriers-passengers
3. FMCSA, *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations* (property vs. passenger comparison table) — https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/regulations/hours-service/summary-hours-service-regulations
4. CFR 2025, Title 49, Vol. 5, § 395.5 (GovInfo PDF) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title49-vol5/pdf/CFR-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-8.pdf
5. FMCSA, *Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service* — https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/sites/fmcsa.dot.gov/files/docs/Interstate-Passenger-Carrying-Driver-Guide-To-HOS.pdf
6. FMCSA Motor Carrier Safety Planner § 6.4.3, *Passenger-Carrying Operations (395.5)* — https://csa.fmcsa.dot.gov/SafetyPlanner/MyFiles/SubSections.aspx?ch=23&sec=69&sub=177

**Caveat on applicability.** These figures are the federal interstate rule. Intrastate operations may be governed by a state's adoption of the federal rules or by a state-specific variant; if the driver never crosses a state line and the state has its own passenger-carrier HOS regime, that regime controls. The three values above are correct as stated for interstate operation under 49 CFR 395.5.

ANSWER — 14 CFR Part 135 flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less

1) Normal requirement: at least 9 consecutive hours of rest. [Ask 1 = 9 hours]
2) Permitted reduction: to 8 consecutive hours, but only with a 10-consecutive-hour make-up rest inside a 24-hour window. [Ask 2 = 8 hours]

Both figures come from 14 CFR 135.273(b), which governs flight attendants in all Part 135 operations (commuter and on-demand alike — the section is not keyed to 135.263/135.265/135.267, which govern flight crewmembers).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. REGULATORY BASIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Applicability. Section 135.273(a) defines "flight attendant" as an individual, other than a flight crewmember, assigned by the certificate holder in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under its operations specifications or in addition to that minimum complement, to duty in an aircraft during flight time. Two consequences:
  - The rule covers both required-complement and extra/optional flight attendants.
  - Whether the operator's aircraft requires a flight attendant under 135.107 (passenger seating configuration, excluding pilot seats, of more than 19) affects whether one must be carried; it does not affect which rest rule applies once a flight attendant is assigned.

"Duty period" under 135.273(a) is the elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment. Rest is therefore measured from actual release to actual report, and it must be consecutive — the rule contains no split-rest provision.

Text (135.273(b)(2)):
  "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

Text (135.273(b)(3)):
  "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. CONDITIONS ON THE 8-HOUR REDUCTION — ALL THREE MUST HOLD
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A certificate holder may schedule, or reduce to, 8 consecutive hours only if all of the following are satisfied:

  (a) The reduced rest is 8 consecutive hours — not 8 hours split, not 8 hours interrupted by duty, phone contact, positioning, or deadhead. Consecutive means consecutive.
  (b) A subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours is actually provided.
  (c) That 10-hour rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period, and it falls between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.

If any condition fails, the floor is 9 hours, not 8. There is no free-standing 8-hour rest for a Part 135 flight attendant.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. WORKED TIMELINE
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Compliant (normal):
  Duty A 07:00-21:00 (14.0 h scheduled). Rest 21:00-06:00 = 9 consecutive hours. Duty B may report 06:00.

Compliant (reduced):
  Duty A 07:00-21:00. Reduced rest 21:00-05:00 = 8 consecutive hours (starts 21:00). Duty B 05:00-15:00. Compensatory rest begins 15:00 = 10 consecutive hours. Deadline check: the 10-hour rest must begin no later than 21:00 the following day (24 hours after 21:00); 15:00 is inside that window. Compliant.

Non-compliant:
  Same Duty A, reduced rest 21:00-05:00, but Duty B runs 05:00-22:00. The compensatory rest would begin 22:00 — after the 21:00 deadline. That is a violation of (b)(3) even though the 8-hour rest itself was 8 hours.

Practical reading: the 8-hour option only works when the duty period following the shortened rest is short enough that the 10-hour make-up rest can start within 24 hours of the start of the shortened rest. In effect the pair costs 18 hours of rest across two nights (8 + 10), which is why most operators schedule the 9-hour norm unless the schedule genuinely supports the pairing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. ENFORCEMENT PROVISIONS (ACTUAL, NOT JUST SCHEDULED)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

135.273(b)(10): no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section.
135.273(b)(11): no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period.

So the rule is both a planning rule (what may be scheduled) and an actual-compliance rule. If a rotation is built on 8 hours and the inbound leg goes mechanical, the flight attendant still may not be assigned until the required rest — 8 hours plus the 10-hour make-up rest on the required schedule — has actually been received. Delays do not shrink the minimum; they push the report time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. WHAT DOES NOT GOVERN THIS ANSWER (COMMON ERRORS)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

  - 135.267 is a flight crewmember rule. Its 10-consecutive-hours-of-rest figure and its 8/9-hour reductions apply to pilots, not to flight attendants. Do not answer "10 hours" for a flight attendant under 135.267.
  - Part 117 does not apply to Part 135 flight attendants. Acclimatization, circadian windows, and the 117 rest tables are Part 121 concepts and are absent from 135.273. There is no time-of-day adjustment in 135.273.
  - 135.273 contains no lodging/suitable-accommodation requirement of its own. Rest must be free of duty (b)(11), but the adequacy of the facility is a matter of company policy, the general operations manual, or a labor agreement, not the rest minimum.
  - Contract, collective bargaining agreement, or fatigue risk management program may exceed these figures. Where it does, the more restrictive provision controls operationally. The regulatory floor is 9, or 8 with the (b)(3) pairing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. THE ONE ALTERNATIVE PATH — 135.273(c) ELECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A certificate holder may, under 135.273(c), apply the flight crewmember flight time and duty limitations and rest requirements of Part 135 to its flight attendants for all operations, provided it establishes written procedures that apply to all flight attendants used in its operation, include the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board are not required), add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flight crewmember above the type-certificate minimum, and are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its operations specifications.

This is an all-or-nothing election requiring FAA-approved procedures and an OpSpec reference; it is not available by informal practice. If — and only if — the operator holds that approval, the rest minimums become flight-time-driven:

  Scheduled flight time      Normal rest     May be reduced to     Required subsequent rest
  less than 8 hours          9 hours         8 hours               at least 10 h, beginning no later than 24 h after the reduced rest begins
  8 or more but under 9 h    10 hours        8 hours               at least 11 h, same 24-h condition
  9 hours or more            11 hours        9 hours               at least 12 h, same 24-h condition

Unless the operator's OpSpecs actually contain the (c) authorization, the answer remains 9 hours / 8 hours.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. IF THE DUTY PERIOD EXCEEDS 14 HOURS (CONTEXT ONLY)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Paragraph (b)(1) caps a scheduled duty period at 14 hours except as provided in (b)(4)-(b)(6), which permit longer scheduled duty periods when flight attendants are assigned in addition to the minimum complement (the text provides for more than 14 up to 16 hours, and more than 16 up to 18 hours, on that basis). Those longer duty periods carry a 12-consecutive-hour rest requirement under (b)(7), reducible to 10 consecutive hours under (b)(8) with a 14-consecutive-hour subsequent rest beginning within the same 24-hour window; (b)(9) further bars scheduling more than 14 duty hours in the 24-hour period commencing after the start of that 10-hour reduced rest. None of this applies to the 14-hours-or-less case in the question.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST FOR THE SCHEDULING/FRM FUNCTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

  1. Confirm the person is a flight attendant within 135.273(a), not a flight crewmember.
  2. Confirm whether an OpSpec under 135.273(c) exists. If yes, use the flight-time table in section 6. If no, use 9/8.
  3. Default build: 9 consecutive hours between release and next report.
  4. If 8 hours is used: verify in the pairing that the 10-hour make-up rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the start of the 8-hour rest, and that it sits between the end of that duty period and the start of the next.
  5. Do not chain two 8-hour rests without the 10-hour make-up rest between them.
  6. Do not schedule any duty — including training, positioning, administrative work, or company-directed communication — inside a required rest period (b)(11).
  7. Record rest and duty in local or UTC consistently, per the 135.273(a) definitions, and retain records sufficient to demonstrate compliance with 135.63 and the operator's GOM/OpSpecs.
  8. On the day of operation, measure rest from actual release. If the actual duty overruns, move the report time; do not shrink the rest.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. ASSUMPTIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------

  - The person is a flight attendant as defined in 135.273(a) and is not acting as a flight crewmember on the rotation.
  - The operator has not elected 135.273(c); if it has, section 6 replaces sections 1-3.
  - The scheduled duty period does not exceed 14 hours; if it does, section 7 applies.
  - No labor agreement, manual, or OpSpec imposes a longer rest; if one does, the longer rest controls.

Final answers restated: 9 consecutive hours normally; reducible to 8 consecutive hours only with a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the reduced rest begins.

# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## Answer

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022 |
| RFCs it obsoletes | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** |

## 1. Current specification — RFC 9113

- **Number:** RFC 9113
- **Title:** *HTTP/2*
- **Date:** June 2022
- **Stream / status:** IETF, Standards Track (Proposed Standard); ISSN 2070-1721
- **Authors/editors:** M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla); C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.)
- **Working group / draft:** HTTPbis WG; `draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis` (published as -07)
- **Authoritative URLs:**
  - https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html (also `.xml`, `.txt`)
  - https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/
- **Abstract (verbatim opening):** "This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). HTTP/2 enables a more efficient use of network resources and a reduced latency by introducing field compression and allowing multiple concurrent exchanges on the same connection. This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

This is the document that replaced the original HTTP/2 specification (RFC 7540, May 2015) and folded in the TLS 1.3 profile (RFC 8740). It is the reference to cite for HTTP/2 today.

## 2. RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113

RFC 9113's front matter carries the header **`Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`**, and its abstract restates the same relationship in prose. The two documents are:

| RFC | Title | Date | Authors | Why it was obsoleted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)* | May 2015 | M. Belshe, R. Peon, M. Thomson (Ed.) | Replaced by the revised HTTP/2 specification (RFC 9113). Appendix B of RFC 9113, "Changes from RFC 7540", enumerates the substantive changes: the RFC 7540 priority scheme is deprecated (frame/field formats retained for interoperability, semantics described only in RFC 7540); the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism for HTTP/2 is deprecated and no longer specified; TLS 1.3 usage now comes from RFC 8740; plus editorial restructuring and alignment with the revised core HTTP semantics. |
| **RFC 8740** | *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2* | February 2020 | B. Schwartz, M. Bishop | Its content was merged into RFC 9113. Appendix B states: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes." |

Obsoletion chain (as recorded in RFC metadata):

```
RFC 7540 (2015) ─┐
                 ├─ obsoleted by ─> RFC 9113 (June 2022)  [current]
RFC 8740 (2020) ─┘
```

Datatracker records this from both directions: RFC 9113 shows "Obsoletes RFC 8740, RFC 7540"; the RFC 7540 document page shows it as obsoleted by RFC 9113.

## 3. Reading of "obsoletes" used here

"Obsoletes" is taken in the **formal RFC-metadata sense** — the `Obsoletes:` header in the document's front matter (the field governed by the RFC Style Guide, RFC 7322), not a loose "supersedes in practice" judgement. Under that reading the answer is closed and exhaustive: exactly two documents, RFC 7540 and RFC 8740. No other RFC appears in that header.

## 4. Explicit boundaries — what RFC 9113 does *not* obsolete

Stated so the answer is not over-read:

- **RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)** is **not** obsoleted. It remains in force and is a normative reference of RFC 9113.
- **RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2)**, which *updates* RFC 7540, is **not** obsoleted by RFC 9113; it remains in effect and is referenced by RFC 9113 for extended CONNECT.
- The **companion HTTP documents published alongside RFC 9113** — RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching), RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1) — obsolete the earlier RFC 7230–7235 series, not HTTP/2. They are outside this question's scope; do not merge their obsoletion lists with RFC 9113's.
- **RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)** is a *successor protocol*, not an obsoletion of HTTP/2. "Obsoleted by" ≠ "succeeded by"; HTTP/2 remains a current, standards-track protocol specified by RFC 9113.
- "Updates" relationships are out of scope by construction: only documents named in the `Obsoletes:` header are listed.

## 5. Verification procedure (re-runnable; "current" is time-sensitive)

Because "current" is indexed to a point in time, re-check before republishing:

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.xml and read the front-matter elements `<obsoletes>` — expected content: `7540`, `8740`.
2. Open https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ and confirm the status line reads "Obsoletes RFC 8740, RFC 7540" and that no "Obsoleted by" / "Updated by" entry has appeared that would displace RFC 9113 as current.
3. Search the RFC Editor index for "HTTP/2" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/search/rfc_search_detail.php?title=HTTP%2F2) and confirm no RFC later than 9113 carries the HTTP/2 specification.
4. Check the RFC 9113 errata page (linked from the RFC Editor info page, https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113) for verified errata that materially change the text; errata do not change the RFC number or the Obsoletes list.
5. If any step disagrees with this answer, the newer document wins — update both the current-RFC number and the obsoletes list together, never one without the other.

## 6. Assumptions recorded

- **Point in time:** "current" = the most recent Standards Track RFC designated as the HTTP/2 specification as of the sources consulted (fetched 2026-11-17). RFC 9113 (June 2022) is that document; no later republication was found.
- **Scope of "obsoletes":** formal `Obsoletes:` metadata only, as argued in §3.
- **Citation depth:** RFC number plus title and date given, so the reader can verify without further lookup.

## 7. One-line citable form

> The current specification of HTTP/2 is RFC 9113 (*HTTP/2*, June 2022, Standards Track), which obsoletes RFC 7540 (*Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, May 2015) and RFC 8740 (*Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*, February 2020).

UK STATUTORY MINIMUM WAGE RATES IN FORCE FROM 1 APRIL 2026

=== HEADLINE ANSWER ===

1. National Living Wage (NLW), workers aged 21 and over, from 1 April 2026: £12.71 per hour (gross).
2. National Minimum Wage (NMW), workers aged 18 to 20, from 1 April 2026: £10.85 per hour (gross).

Both are gross hourly rates in pounds sterling, quoted to the penny as set by the amending instrument. No rounding or conversion has been applied.

=== EFFECTIVE DATE AND PERIOD OF APPLICATION ===

Both rates take effect on 1 April 2026 and remain the statutory minimum rates until the next annual uprating on 1 April 2027. 'From April 2026' is therefore read as the rate in force from the first day of April 2026, not an average or a mid-month figure. The rates are UK-wide: the instrument extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and there are no devolved variations in the statutory minimum wage.

=== LEGAL BASIS (PRIMARY SOURCE) ===

The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, S.I. 2026/357, made 19 March 2026, coming into force 1 April 2026, amending the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (S.I. 2015/621):

- Regulation 2(2): in regulation 4 (the national living wage), for '£12.21' substitute '£12.71'. This is the 21-and-over rate.
- Regulation 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b), for '£10.00' substitute '£10.85'. Per the Explanatory Note, regulation 4A(1)(b) covers 'workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21)'.
- Regulation 2(3)(b) and (c): under-18 rate and apprentice rate each raised from £7.55 to £8.00 (outside the scope of this request).
- Regulation 2(4): accommodation offset raised from £10.66 to £11.10 per day (context only; not a wage rate).

The Explanatory Note states expressly: 'Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour' and 'Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour.'

=== CORROBORATION (THREE INDEPENDENT PUBLISHERS, IDENTICAL FIGURES) ===

- GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates' table, row 'April 2026': 21 and over = £12.71; 18 to 20 = £10.85.
- Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (published 1 April 2026), and the GOV.UK press release 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour': National Living Wage (21 and over) £12.71 (+£0.50, +4.1%); 18-20 Year Old Rate £10.85 (+£0.85, +8.5%).
- ONS, Low and high pay in the UK (ASHE, April 2026 reference date): 'On the ASHE reference date in April 2026, the NMW and NLW rates were: £12.71 for employees aged 21 years and over; £10.85 for employees aged 18 to 20 years.'

These are enacted rates, not projections: the instrument was made on 19 March 2026 and the LPC confirms the increases 'come into force from 1 April 2026' following recommendations submitted 27 October 2025 and accepted at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.

=== AGE-BAND VERIFICATION ===

The NLW applies to workers aged 21 and over in 2026. The LPC's own note records the threshold history: NLW applied at 25+ from April 2016, fell to 23+ in April 2021, and to 21+ in April 2024. The 21+ band is therefore correct for the April 2026 uprating; figures from earlier years (e.g. the 23+ or 25+ bands) must not be used. Workers aged 20 and under remain on the National Minimum Wage age bands.

=== SCOPE AND EXCLUSIONS ===

In scope and answered: 21+ NLW; 18-20 NMW.
Out of scope, stated only to prevent misattribution: the 16-17 rate and the apprentice rate (both £8.00 from 1 April 2026) and the daily accommodation offset (£11.10). None of these are the figures requested.

Not to be confused with the statutory rates: the 'Real Living Wage' published by the Living Wage Foundation is a separate voluntary benchmark set by a campaign body, is not statute, and is not the figure answered here.

=== BASIS OF QUOTATION ===

Gross pay, before tax and National Insurance, per hour actually worked, as defined by the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015. Rates are as printed in the statute to the nearest penny; no arithmetic was performed, so there is no rounding risk. Certain categories (apprentices in the first year or under 19, some trainees, participants in work trials, and workers receiving living accommodation with an offset applied) are subject to different rules and should not be assumed to be on the headline figures above.

REGULATORY ANSWER — FMCSA short-haul exception, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)

BOTTOM LINE
1. Radius: the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation itself states the conversion: 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles.
2. Release: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

GOVERNING TEXT (quoted, current eCFR; identical in the 2024 printed CFR, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)):
"(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
 (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
 (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
 (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
 (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
 (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

SCOPE NOTE (resolves the property/passenger ambiguity without blocking): subparagraph (ii) — the 150-air-mile radius and the 14-consecutive-hour return/release rule — is identical for property-carrying and passenger-carrying CMV drivers. The only property/passenger split in (e)(1) is the off-duty requirement in (iii): 10 consecutive hours off duty for property-carrying, 8 for passenger-carrying. Both requested values therefore hold either way.

HOW TO APPLY THE TWO LIMITS
A. Radius — measurement.
 - "Air mile" is a nautical mile (6,076 ft); 1 air mile ≈ 1.15078 statute miles, hence 150 air miles ≈ 172.6 statute miles. Use the air-mile figure as the test; the 172.6-mile figure is the same limit expressed in statute miles, not a separate or larger allowance.
 - The radius is a straight-line (great-circle) distance from the normal work reporting location to the furthest point the vehicle operates — not route mileage, not driving distance, not a return-trip radius. A driver who stays within 150 air miles as the crow flies qualifies on distance even if the road route is longer; a driver who exceeds 150 air miles straight-line fails even if the odometer shows less.
 - "Normal work reporting location" is the fixed location where the driver reports to and is released from work. It is the anchor for both the radius and the return requirement.
 - Practical check: draw a 150-air-mile (172.6-statute-mile) circle centered on the normal work reporting location; every point of the day's operation must fall inside it.

B. Release — measurement.
 - The clock starts when the driver comes on duty and runs 14 consecutive hours. By hour 14 the driver must be back at the normal work reporting location and released from work. Off-duty time does not pause or extend this 14-hour period.
 - "Released from work" means the driver is relieved of duty at that location; merely being back in the yard but still on duty does not satisfy it.
 - Caveat in the text: the return-and-release condition in (ii) does not apply to a driver-salesperson (the radius and off-duty conditions still do).

C. Limits that are NOT relaxed by this exception (state these alongside the answer so 14 hours is not misread as 14 hours of driving):
 - The driver must still comply with 49 CFR 395.3 hours-of-service limits: 11-hour driving limit, the 14th-hour driving window, and the 60/70-hour limit in 7/8 consecutive days. FMCSA's Drivers' Guide to HOS states plainly: 'Drivers utilizing the short-haul exception continue to be limited to 11 hours of driving time.'
 - What the exception removes is the record-of-duty-status obligation: exemption from § 395.8 (RODS) and § 395.11 (supporting documents). That is why time records substitute for a log.
 - Secondary point, outside the two asks: FMCSA's published summary table lists the 30-minute rest break as not applicable to the 150-air-mile short-haul driver, while the regulatory text of (e)(1) itself names only §§ 395.8 and 395.11. Treat the 30-minute-break question as a separate compliance determination, not part of this answer.

CONDITIONS — the exception is not automatic; all must be met every day
1. Operation within 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location.
2. Return to the normal work reporting location and release from work within 14 consecutive hours (driver-salespersons excepted from this condition).
3. At least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty (property-carrying) or 8 consecutive hours (passenger-carrying).
4. The employing motor carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records showing: time the driver reports for duty each day; total hours on duty each day; time released from duty each day; and, for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, the total time for the preceding 7 days per § 395.8(j)(2).

FAILURE CONSEQUENCE
If any condition is not met on a given day (radius exceeded, not released within 14 consecutive hours, off-duty period short, or required time records not kept), the exception is unavailable for that day and the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day. FMCSA's guidance: 'If the individual cannot meet the terms of the exception (e.g., the driver goes beyond the distance limitation or works too many hours), the driver must complete a RODS for that day as soon as' practicable — i.e., reconstruct the day's record; the exemption does not apply retroactively.

DISTINCT PROVISIONS — do not confuse with the answer above
 - 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2) (non-CDL property-carrying short-haul): also a 150 air-mile radius, but the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour, may not drive after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days nor after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7, and such drivers are ineligible for (e)(1), (g) and (o). Its 16-hour allowance is not the answer to ask 2.
 - 49 CFR 395.1(o) (16-hour adverse/split provision): return and release within 16 hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, limited to once per 6 consecutive days after 5 prior qualifying duty tours. Not the short-haul RODS exception.
 - 49 CFR 395.1(p) (motion picture production sites): a 100 air-mile radius. The 100-mile figure is a different provision and does not apply here.
 - 49 CFR 395.1(g) sleeper-berth and the split-sleeper provisions are likewise separate.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR CITATION IN A POLICY OR SOP: 'Under 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), a driver is relieved of the RODS requirement only if the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location and returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours, with at least 10 consecutive hours off duty (property-carrying; 8 for passenger-carrying) separating each 14 hours on duty and the carrier retaining 6 months of time records.'

BASIS: current eCFR text of 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) (sha256 1f7674313f0d) and the 2024 printed CFR, title 49, vol. 5 (sha256 a03f87b5824e), which agree verbatim; FMCSA Drivers' Guide to HOS (Apr. 2022) and FMCSA Summary of Hours of Service Regulations corroborate the 150 air-mile / 14-consecutive-hour formulation. Figures above are quoted from the regulation, not recalled.
