question: M11
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1))

ANSWERS
1. Radius: 150 air miles (the regulation's own parenthetical conversion: 172.6 statute miles) from the normal work reporting location. — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i)
2. Release: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii)

CONTROLLING TEXT (current eCFR, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), fetched 2026-11-17)
"(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) total hours on-duty each day; (C) time released from duty each day; and (D) total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

RULE VERSION PIN
These figures are the post-2020 HOS final rule values (compliance date 29 September 2020), which raised the short-haul radius from 100 to 150 air miles and the duty period from 12 to 14 hours. Any citation to a pre-2020 edition (100 air miles / 12 hours) is superseded and must not be used.

SCOPE AND VARIANTS
- The 150/14 pair in (e)(1) applies to both property-carrying and passenger-carrying CMV drivers. The only difference is the intervening off-duty period: 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying. Both variants carry the same 150 air-mile radius and the same 14-consecutive-hour release.
- Do not confuse this with § 395.1(e)(2), the non-CDL property-carrying provision: it also uses a 150 air-mile radius, but it requires return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour and caps driving at the 14th hour on 5 of 7 days and the 16th hour on 2 of 7 days. It is not a flat "released within 14 consecutive hours" rule and does not answer this question.
- Driver-salespersons: the return-and-release condition in (e)(1)(ii) is expressly inapplicable to a driver-salesperson; the 150 air-mile radius condition in (e)(1)(i) still applies.

WHAT THE EXCEPTION DOES AND DOES NOT RELIEVE
- Relieved: the records-of-duty-status requirement (§ 395.8) and the ELD requirement (§ 395.11). Qualifying drivers also are not required to take the 30-minute break under § 395.1(e)(1).
- Not relieved: the substantive driving and on-duty limits of § 395.3 (11-hour driving limit, 14-hour driving window for property carriers, 60/70-hour limit) remain in force. Note the interaction for passenger carriers: § 395.3 permits 15 hours on duty, but a passenger-carrying driver claiming (e)(1) must still be released within 14 consecutive hours, so the exception is the tighter constraint.

MEASUREMENT AND VERIFICATION PROCEDURE
1. Fix the normal work reporting location for the duty tour — the location where the driver reports to and is released from work. Per FMCSA guidance, this location may differ from shift to shift provided the driver starts and ends each shift at the same location.
2. Measure the radius as a straight-line (great-circle) distance in air miles — 1 air mile = 1 nautical mile = 1.15078 statute miles — from that location to the farthest point the vehicle reaches during the tour. 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles. Do not use route/driving distance; the regulation measures air miles, and the statute-mile figure is only the converted equivalent.
3. Measure the 14 hours from the moment the driver comes on duty (report time) to the moment the carrier releases the driver from duty at the work reporting location. Both events — the return and the release — must fall inside the same 14-consecutive-hour window. Off-duty time inside the tour does not extend that window.
4. Evidence file per driver-day: report time, total hours on duty, release time, and total time for the preceding 7 days for new or intermittent drivers. Retain 6 months.

FALLBACK / TRIGGERS (exception forfeited for the day)
- The driver exceeds 150 air miles from the normal work reporting location at any point in the tour, or
- the driver is not returned to that location and released within 14 consecutive hours, or
- the required off-duty period (10 hours property / 8 hours passenger) is not taken between tours.
On any of these, the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day (paper log or ELD) and the carrier must retain it; the time-record substitute is no longer sufficient. Adverse driving conditions do not cure a missed 14-hour release — FMCSA's guidance is that a short-haul driver who cannot return within 14 hours must record duty status for that day. Separately, a driver who has used the short-haul exception on more than 8 days in the last 30 days must use an ELD to record time for that day.

OPEN ITEMS OUTSIDE THIS DETERMINATION
- State-level adaptations and carrier policy may impose shorter windows or smaller radii; this determination states the federal floor only.
- Nothing here addresses Canadian or Mexican analogues.

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT OPERATING LIMITS (US, 14 CFR part 68 / § 61.113(i))

BOTTOM LINE — the three limits, as currently in force:

| Limit | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum takeoff weight | 12,500 lb | 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) |
| Occupants the aircraft may be AUTHORIZED to carry | 7 occupants | 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) |
| Passengers ON BOARD | 6 passengers | 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) |

Plus one categorical exclusion in the same sentence: the aircraft must NOT be a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29.

1. CONTROLLING REGULATORY TEXT

14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) (current eCFR, amended through Amdt. 61-159, 90 FR 35218, July 24, 2025) provides that a private pilot may act as PIC or required flightcrew member without a part 67 medical certificate if the pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets § 61.23(c)(3), and complies with all of the following conditions and limitations:

  "(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; and
   (2) The flight, including each portion of the flight, is not carried out—
     (i) At an altitude that is more than 18,000 feet above mean sea level;
     (ii) Outside the United States unless authorized by the country in which the flight is conducted; or
     (iii) At an indicated airspeed exceeding 250 knots; and
   (3) The pilot has available in his or her logbook—
     (i) The completed medical examination checklist required under § 68.7 of this chapter; and
     (ii) The certificate of course completion required under § 61.23(c)(3)."

FAA corroboration, BasicMed airman page (faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med):
  Aircraft Requirements — "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants"; "Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds."
  Operating Requirements — "Carries not more than six passengers."

Statutory basis: BasicMed was created by § 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (PL 114-190), implemented through 14 CFR part 68 and § 61.113(i). The aircraft limits above are the expanded figures mandated by § 828 ("Expansion of BasicMed") of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63), effective November 12, 2024.

2. WHAT EACH FIGURE MEANS — AND WHY THE THREE ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE

(a) 12,500 lb — MAXIMUM TAKEOFF WEIGHT. This is the aircraft's maximum (certificated) takeoff weight as established by its design approval — type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended TC — or, for experimental aircraft issued a special airworthiness certificate, as determined in the operating limitations established by the operator. It is a hard ceiling: the aircraft's MTOW must be 12,500 lb or less. If an aircraft was certificated above 12,500 lb and is altered (via STC/ATC) to a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 12,500 lb or less, it then qualifies. Note that § 61.113(i)(1) does not relieve the aircraft from its own operating limitations; where an operating limitation is more restrictive, the more restrictive limitation governs.

(b) 7 OCCUPANTS — AUTHORIZED OCCUPANCY. This is a property of the AIRCRAFT, not of the flight: the number of occupants the aircraft is AUTHORIZED to carry under federal law (design approval, or the operating limitations for experimental aircraft). It includes the pilot and any required flightcrew. An aircraft whose approval authorizes 8 or more occupants does not qualify at all, regardless of how many people actually get in. An aircraft type-certificated for more than 7 occupants may be made eligible by alteration under a new design approval (STC or ATC) that reduces authorized occupancy to 7 or fewer.

(c) 6 PASSENGERS — ACTUAL LOAD. This is a property of the FLIGHT: the number of passengers actually on board may not exceed 6. Read together with (b):
  - Single-pilot-certificated aircraft: 1 pilot + up to 6 passengers = 7 occupants — the maximum use of both limits.
  - Two-pilot-certificated aircraft (two required flightcrew): 2 required pilots + up to 5 passengers = 7 occupants.
  - Occupants other than the PIC operating under BasicMed may be passengers, required pilot flightcrew members, or a flight instructor giving instruction; a non-required pilot who is neither required flightcrew nor an instructor providing instruction counts as a passenger.

So: 7 is the certification-side ceiling (who the aircraft may carry), 6 is the operations-side ceiling (who is actually carried). Both must be satisfied on every flight; satisfying one does not excuse the other.

3. IMPORTANT — SUPERSEDED FIGURES TO NOT USE

The pre-November 12, 2024 limits were: 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight, aircraft authorized to carry not more than 6 occupants, and not more than 5 passengers on board. Those figures still appear in:
  - FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1A (5/3/17), §§ 3.2, 5.1.1, 5.1.3, 5.2.1 (6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers);
  - FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1 (1/9/17) (same);
  - the printed 2024 edition of 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) on govinfo (6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers);
  - FAA Notice N 8000.386, which recites them as the "before" set.
They are obsolete. Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24) states the transition explicitly: "Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board." Any answer using 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers is out of date for flights on or after 11/12/2024.

4. PRACTITIONER NOTES / VERIFICATION ITEMS

- These three aircraft limits are only one element of BasicMed eligibility. The other conditions — at or below 18,000 ft MSL, within the US (or a country where BasicMed is authorized), indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots, no compensation or hire, plus the driver's license, prior-medical-after-7/14/2006, CMEC, physician exam, and online course requirements — are outside the scope of this question but operate cumulatively. An aircraft that meets 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers can still be flown outside BasicMed's privileges if any of the other conditions is breached.
- 14 CFR § 91.319(j) governs experimental aircraft operated under BasicMed and historically mirrored the occupant ceiling. The version of § 91.319(j) quoted in the 2017 ACs reflects the pre-expansion six-occupant figure; the current text should be checked against eCFR before relying on a specific number for experimental aircraft. The rule of construction is that the experimental aircraft's special airworthiness operating limitations control, and they cannot be more permissive than § 61.113(i)(1).
- Verification: confirm the current text of § 61.113(i)(1) and § 91.319(j) on eCFR before each use, since the part 61 amendment history shows frequent changes (most recently Amdt. 61-158, 89 FR 90577, 11/18/2024 and Amdt. 61-159, 90 FR 35218, 7/24/2025).

question: M3
answer:
# Hours of service for a passenger-carrying CMV driver (US federal, interstate)

**Scope of this answer:** current US federal FMCSA hours-of-service rules for a *passenger-carrying* commercial motor vehicle (motorcoach/bus) operated by an interstate motor carrier — 49 CFR Part 395, specifically § 395.5. These are the three per-duty-period limits asked for. Weekly cumulative caps and the exceptions that can move the numbers are noted separately below so they are not confused with the base answers.

## 1. The three answers

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** of driving, following 8 consecutive hours off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours** off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15 hours** on duty, following 8 consecutive hours off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2) |

Controlling text, § 395.5(a) (verbatim, eCFR):

> "Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1: (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle: (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

Note the structure: the 8-hour off-duty period is the *reset* that starts a fresh 10-hour driving allotment and a fresh 15-hour on-duty count. It is **8** consecutive hours for passenger-carrying vehicles, not 10 (10 is the property-carrying figure, § 395.3(a)(1)).

## 2. How the three limits interact

Both per-shift limits run simultaneously; **whichever is reached first stops driving.** Driving is capped at 10 hours, and driving is also prohibited once on-duty time reaches 15 hours, even if fewer than 10 hours have been spent driving. Two consequences that are commonly missed:

- **The 15-hour limit is a cumulative on-duty clock, not an elapsed 15-hour window.** Off-duty time is not counted in the 15-hour period (FMCSA summary for passenger-carrying drivers: "Off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour period"). A mid-shift off-duty break therefore pushes the 15-on-duty-hour point later on the clock. This is the key structural difference from the property-carrying 14-hour window, which off-duty time does *not* extend.
- **Reaching either limit bars driving only, not other work.** After 10 driving hours or 15 on-duty hours the driver may not drive, but the regulation does not by itself forbid continued on-duty non-driving work. Practically, though, that work consumes the 15-hour on-duty budget and must be logged.

## 3. Worked example (shows both limits and the reset)

Driver reports for duty at 06:00.

| Clock | Activity | Cumulative driving | Cumulative on-duty |
|---|---|---|---|
| 06:00–08:00 | Driving | 2.0 | 2.0 |
| 08:00–09:00 | On duty, not driving | 2.0 | 3.0 |
| 09:00–12:00 | Driving | 5.0 | 6.0 |
| 12:00–13:00 | **Off duty** (not counted toward 15) | 5.0 | 6.0 |
| 13:00–17:00 | Driving | 9.0 | 10.0 |
| 17:00–18:00 | On duty, not driving | 9.0 | 11.0 |
| 18:00–19:00 | Driving | **10.0** | 12.0 |

At 19:00 the driver has used exactly 10.0 driving hours (the cap — no further driving) while having accumulated only 12.0 of the 15 on-duty hours. **The 10-hour driving limit binds first.** The driver may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken; going off duty at 19:00, the earliest new driving allotment begins at 03:00 the next day.

Variant showing the 15-hour limit binding: if the same driver had accumulated 15 on-duty hours (e.g., 6 on-duty hours before the 12:00–13:00 off-duty break plus 9 on-duty hours after it, reaching 15 at 22:00 on the clock) with only 8 driving hours, driving would be barred from 22:00 onward by § 395.5(a)(2).

## 4. What counts as on-duty and off-duty (this is what makes the numbers move)

- **On-duty time, § 395.2:** all time from when the driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until relieved from work and all responsibility for performing work. It includes waiting time in readiness, loading/unloading and passenger handling, inspection, and **other compensated work for a non-motor-carrier employer**. All compensated work counts.
- **Off-duty time:** not separately defined; in effect, any time that is not driving time, on-duty time, or sleeper-berth time. FMCSA's guidelines require, for meal and routine stops to be off duty, that the driver be **relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus/CMV, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight it is carrying.** A driver who stays with the coach and remains responsible for passengers is not off duty.
- **Travel/cushioning time, § 395.1(j):** travel at the carrier's direction but not driving and not assuming other responsibility counts as on-duty **unless** the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case the whole period may be recorded as off duty. Relief-driver travel to a layover works the same way.

## 5. Exceptions that can lawfully move the three numbers

Apply only by their own terms; do not build them into the baseline.

1. **Adverse driving conditions** — FMCSA's passenger-carrier summary states drivers may extend the 10-hour maximum driving time and the 15-hour on-duty limit by **up to 2 hours** when adverse driving conditions (as defined in § 395.2) are encountered; § 395.1(b) is the operative provision. Verify the current § 395.1(b) text for the exact conditions and any post-run off-duty requirement before relying on it.
2. **Sleeper berth, § 395.1(g)(3)** — a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth (defined in § 393.76) may accumulate the **equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty** by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. As FMCSA summarizes it: at least 8 hours in the sleeper berth, splittable into two periods **neither less than 2 hours**, and the pairing must total at least 8 hours. Read the subparagraph text before using a split.
3. **Other § 395.1 exemptions** — the regulation is expressly "subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1." If the operation relies on any of them, confirm it by its own terms and keep the supporting documentation.

## 6. What does NOT apply to passenger-carrying drivers (common, expensive error)

These are **property-carrying** rules in § 395.3 and the 2020 flexibility amendments, and they do not set the limits for a motorcoach:

- 11-hour driving limit (§ 395.3(a)(1)) — passenger limit is 10.
- 14-hour driving window (§ 395.3(a)(2)) — passenger limit is 15 on-duty hours, with off-duty time excluded.
- 30-minute break after 8 cumulative driving hours (§ 395.3(a)(3)(ii)) — a property-carrying requirement; it is not part of § 395.5.
- 34-hour restart (§ 395.3(c)) — property-carrying; § 395.5(b) contains no restart provision for passenger carriers.
- The 2-hour/7-hour split of the 10-hour off-duty period — that is the property-carrying sleeper split; the passenger split runs off the 8-hour requirement in § 395.1(g)(3).
- The 150-air-mile short-haul exception in § 395.1(e) is written for property-carrying CMV drivers and does not relieve a passenger-carrying driver of § 395.5.

## 7. Weekly cumulative caps (for completeness — not answers to asks 1–3)

Separately from the per-shift limits, § 395.5(b) bars driving after the driver has been on duty, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services:

- **60 hours in any 7 consecutive days** if the employing carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- **70 hours in any 8 consecutive days** if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.

A passenger carrier may use either cycle. These are cumulative caps, not per-shift limits, and there is no 34-hour restart available under § 395.5.

## 8. "Per day/shift" — no 24-hour reset

The limits attach to a **duty period**, not to a calendar day or a fixed 24-hour window. There is no rule that a driver is refreshed at midnight or after 24 hours; only **8 consecutive hours off duty** starts a new 10-hour/15-hour cycle, and the 60/70-hour caps are measured on rolling 7/8-day periods.

## 9. Jurisdiction caveat

The values above are the **federal** baseline for an interstate carrier. Intrastate-only passenger operations may be governed by state hours-of-service rules (some states, e.g. California, impose their own intrastate limits), and a state may be **stricter** than the federal rule where it applies. Before publishing these numbers as an operating policy, confirm (a) that the carrier is subject to federal rules rather than a state intrastate regime, and (b) whether any state in which the driver operates imposes a lower limit. A stricter state rule would reduce the three values, never raise them.

## 10. Records to support the numbers

Driver's record of duty status under § 395.8 (ELD for most passenger carriers and drivers required to keep RODS), retained **6 months** per § 395.1(e)-style time-record requirements and § 395.8; for multiple-employer/intermittent drivers, a signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty (§ 395.8(j)). Compensated work for any employer counts as on-duty.

## 11. Citations

- 49 CFR § 395.5(a)(1)–(2) — 10 hours driving / 8 consecutive hours off duty; no driving after 15 hours on duty. (70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005; text unchanged in the eCFR snapshot consulted.)
- 49 CFR § 395.5(b)(1)–(2) — 60-hour/7-day and 70-hour/8-day on-duty caps.
- 49 CFR § 395.2 — definitions of on-duty time, driving time, sleeper berth, adverse driving conditions.
- 49 CFR § 395.1(b) (adverse driving conditions), § 395.1(g)(3) (passenger sleeper berth), § 395.1(j) (travel time).

**Bottom line:** a motorcoach driver may drive **10 hours** after **8 consecutive hours off duty**, and may not drive after being on duty **15 hours** following those 8 consecutive hours off duty — whichever limit is reached first.

answer:
BOTTOM LINE

Under 14 CFR Part 135, a flight attendant who is scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less must receive a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. That rest may be scheduled at, or reduced to, 8 consecutive hours — but only if the flight attendant is then given a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours that is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.

| Element | Value | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Rest owed after a scheduled duty period of 14 h or less | 9 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(2) |
| Minimum to which that rest may be reduced | 8 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Compensatory rest triggered by the 8-hour reduction | at least 10 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Deadline for the compensatory rest to begin | no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Required placement of both rests | between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | §135.273(b)(2), (b)(3) |

1. THE BASE REQUIREMENT — 9 CONSECUTIVE HOURS

§135.273(b)(1) bars assigning a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours (except under the augmented-crew paragraphs (b)(4)–(b)(6)). §135.273(b)(2) then provides that a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less 'must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours,' which 'must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.' The FAA's published FAQ states the same: with a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest is required before the next duty period.

Two points operators routinely get wrong:

- The 9 hours is keyed to the DUTY PERIOD, not to flight time. Unlike the flight-crewmember table in §135.265(b) (9/10/11 hours depending on scheduled flight time), §135.273 imposes a flat 9-hour minimum for any duty period of 14 hours or less. A four-hour duty day still generates 9 hours of rest for a flight attendant covered by §135.273.
- It is 'scheduled rest,' i.e., a rest period built into the assignment. §135.273(b)(10) prohibits assigning a flight attendant to any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section, and (b)(11) prohibits assigning a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period. The regulation does not prescribe where the rest is taken or require a rest facility for flight attendants; it requires consecutive hours free of duty.

2. THE REDUCTION — DOWN TO 8 CONSECUTIVE HOURS, WITH A PRICE

§135.273(b)(3): 'The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'

The reduction is therefore conditional, and all four elements must be satisfied:

(a) The reduced rest is at least 8 consecutive hours — 8 is the floor; (b)(3) authorizes no shorter rest, and there is no provision in §135.273 permitting anything less for a 14-hour-or-less duty period.
(b) A subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours is provided.
(c) That subsequent rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.
(d) Both rests fall between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Note that (b)(3) says 'scheduled or reduced.' The 8-hour rest may be planned in the pairing/crew schedule up front, or the 9-hour rest may be reduced in real time; either path triggers the full compensatory-rest obligation. There is no 'one-time' or 'discretionary' reduction that escapes the 10-hour makeup rest.

Worked timeline. Duty period ends 2100 on Day 1.
- Normal case: 9 consecutive hours of rest, 2100 Day 1 to 0600 Day 2; next duty may report at 0600 Day 2.
- Reduced case: 8 consecutive hours of rest, 2100 Day 1 to 0500 Day 2 (reduced rest begins 2100 Day 1). The subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours must BEGIN no later than 2100 Day 2 (24 hours after 2100 Day 1) and must run between the end of the Day 2 duty period and the start of the next duty period. A Day 2 duty period of 0500–1400 followed by rest beginning 1400 Day 2 satisfies the requirement (1400 is earlier than the 2100 Day 2 deadline). A Day 2 duty period of 0500–2200 would not, because the 10-hour rest could not begin until 2200, after the 2100 deadline.

3. WHAT THE ANSWER IS NOT — THREE BOUNDARIES

- It is not 12 hours. The 12-hour base rest (reducible to 10 hours) in §135.273(b)(7)–(b)(8) belongs to the regime for scheduled duty periods exceeding 14 hours under the augmented-crew paragraphs, which are outside the question asked. Do not import those figures into a 14-hour-or-less duty period.
- It is not the §135.265(c) flight-crewmember reduction table (8/8/9 hours keyed to scheduled flight time) unless the operator has made the §135.273(c) election described below.
- The §135.273(b)(9) restriction — that after a 10-hour reduction the certificate holder may not schedule a flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest period — is triggered only by a (b)(8) 10-hour reduction. It is not triggered by the 8-hour reduction under (b)(3), though the 24-hour deadline in (b)(3) achieves a similar scheduling constraint.

4. APPLICABILITY CHECKS BEFORE THE NUMBER IS RELIED ON

- Is the person an assigned flight attendant? §135.273 applies to certificate holders that assign flight attendants to duty. §135.107 requires a flight attendant crewmember on aircraft with a passenger seating configuration, excluding any pilot seat, of more than 19. Confirm against the applicability paragraph of §135.273 and the operator's ops specs whether a particular cabin attendant is a flight attendant 'assigned to duty' within the rule; a non-crew cabin aide or passenger is outside it.
- Has the operator elected §135.273(c)? A certificate holder may instead apply the subpart F flight-crewmember flight time and duty limitations and rest requirements to flight attendants for all operations, provided it establishes written procedures that apply to all its flight attendants, incorporate the subpart F requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board not required), add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each excess flight crewmember, and are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its operations specifications. Under that election the answer changes: rest is keyed to scheduled flight time under §135.265(b) (9 consecutive hours for less than 8 hours scheduled flight time; 10 for 8 but less than 9; 11 for 9 or more), reducible under §135.265(c) to 8, 8, or 9 hours respectively, with compensatory rests of 10, 11, or 12 hours beginning no later than 24 hours after commencement of the reduced rest. If the operator has this election, the governing numbers come from its approved procedures and ops specs, not from (b)(2)–(b)(3).
- More restrictive sources. A collective bargaining agreement, the company manual/GOM, an approved fatigue risk management program, or an ops-spec limitation may impose rest longer than 9 hours or forbid the 8-hour reduction. Those sources are a floor above the regulation; they cannot lawfully authorize less than 9 hours, or less than 8 hours with the compensatory rest, for a flight attendant covered by §135.273(b).
- Exemptions/deviation. If the operator holds an exemption or deviation affecting crew rest, read it; absent one, the (b)(2)–(b)(3) scheme governs. The analysis here assumes none.
- Scheduled versus actual. The rule is written in terms of the SCHEDULED duty period and SCHEDULED rest period. The schedule must comply on its face. If actual duty runs beyond the scheduled period so that the flight attendant is actually on duty more than 14 hours, the assignment falls outside (b)(1)–(b)(3) and the operator must look to the augmented-crew paragraphs (b)(4)–(b)(7) (12 consecutive hours of rest, reducible to 10 under (b)(8), with the (b)(9) 14-hour cap on the following duty period), plus any manual provisions on revising schedules in real time.

5. DOCUMENTATION

Build the 9-hour rest (or the 8-hour rest plus the 10-hour makeup rest, with its 24-hour deadline) into the published crew schedule and pairing records, and track report and release times so that actual duty can be compared with scheduled duty. Retain duty/rest records consistent with §135.63 recordkeeping and the manual requirements applicable to the certificate holder, and record the compensatory rest explicitly whenever the 8-hour reduction is used, including the clock time the reduced rest began and the clock time the 10-hour rest is scheduled to begin, so the 24-hour test is auditable.

6. ONE-SENTENCE ANSWER

Nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, reducible to eight consecutive hours only if a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest, with both rests falling between the end of the scheduled duty period and the start of the next duty period (§135.273(b)(2)–(b)(3)).

The first reads: "(b)(1) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 10 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commencement of the reduced rest pe- riod."

# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## Answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, IETF Standards Track (Proposed Standard), M. Thomson and C. Benfield (Eds.) |
| 2. RFCs that RFC 9113 obsoletes | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** |

## 1. Current specification: RFC 9113

RFC 9113 is the document that currently specifies HTTP/2. Evidence from the RFC Editor's own metadata and text (fetched 2026-11-17T05:39:43Z):

- Title and date block: "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 ... June 2022. M. Thomson, Ed., C. Benfield, Ed. Proposed Standard" (rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113).
- Document header fields: "Stream: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) / RFC: 9113 / Obsoletes: 7540, 8740 / Category: Standards Track / Published: June 2022 / ISSN: 2070-1721" (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html).
- Abstract: "This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2)."

Corroboration that RFC 9113 has superseded the older document: the RFC Editor's info page for RFC 7540 carries the banner "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113." That is the obsoleted-by direction of the same chain, so the two records agree.

Currency check: as of the fetched page state (2026-11-17T05:39:43Z) the RFC 9113 info page shows no "obsoleted by" or "updated by" supersession banner, i.e. RFC 9113 was still the current HTTP/2 specification at fetch time. Because the answer is date-sensitive, the fetch timestamp is stated here so the claim can be re-verified against https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 rather than taken on trust.

## 2. RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113

RFC 9113 obsoletes exactly two RFCs:

1. **RFC 7540** — *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, May 2015, Standards Track, M. Belshe, R. Peon, M. Thomson (Ed.). This was the original HTTP/2 specification. It is now obsolete per the RFC Editor banner: "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113."
2. **RFC 8740** — *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*. RFC 9113 Appendix B ("Changes from RFC 7540") states: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes." RFC 8740 was a narrow update to RFC 7540's TLS requirements, so its content is folded into RFC 9113 rather than left standing as a separate update.

Primary evidence, verbatim:

- Abstract of RFC 9113: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
- Header field: "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740".
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 7540: "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113. This RFC was updated, see RFC 8740."

## Terminology note (why the list has exactly two entries)

In RFC metadata, **Obsoletes** and **Updates** are distinct relations:

- *Obsoletes* means the newer document wholly replaces the older one, which should no longer be implemented or cited as current.
- *Updates* means the newer document amends specific parts of the older one while the older one remains in force.

RFC 7540 was both **updated by** RFC 8740 and **obsoleted by** RFC 9113 — these are two separate recorded facts, and only the second is what ask 2 requests. Consistently, RFC 9113's own obsoletes list contains 7540 and 8740 and nothing else; it does not list RFC 9110, RFC 9111, or RFC 9112. Those documents from the 2022 HTTP specification refactoring are related context (HTTP semantics, caching, HTTP/1.1 message syntax) but are not part of the HTTP/2 obsoletes chain, and they are deliberately excluded from the answer.

## Scope notes

- The question concerns HTTP/2 as standardized by the IETF. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) and QUIC are separate protocols and are not successors that obsolete HTTP/2; RFC 9113's obsoletes list confirms this.
- RFC 9113 does not obsolete the HTTP/1.1 message syntax; it is an alternative expression of HTTP semantics over a different framing layer.
- RFC 9113 deprecates, but does not delete, parts of RFC 7540: the priority scheme is deprecated (PRIORITY frame format and priority fields retained, semantics still described only in RFC 7540, with [HTTP-PRIORITY] recommended instead), and the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism is removed from the specification and the `HTTP2-Settings` header field registration is marked obsoleted. These are content changes inside the obsoletion, not additional obsoleted RFCs.

HR BRIEFING NOTE — UK National Living Wage / National Minimum Wage rates effective 1 April 2026

1. THE TWO FIGURES REQUESTED

| Band | Statutory hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 March 2026) | Increase |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | £12.71 | £12.21 | £0.50 (4.1%) |
| National Minimum Wage — workers aged 18 to 20 | £10.85 | £10.00 | £0.85 (8.5%) |

Both are gross hourly rates in pounds sterling. They apply from 1 April 2026 (not merely 'April 2026'); the previous rates ran to and including 31 March 2026.

2. FULL RATE TABLE FOR THE SAME UPRATING (needed because payroll cannot apply one band in isolation)

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 |
|---|---|
| National Living Wage, 21 and over | £12.71 |
| 18 to 20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 |
| 16 to 17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 |
| Accommodation offset (max daily deduction) | £11.10 per day |

3. LEGAL BASIS — these are enacted rates, not proposals

- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357. Made 19 March 2026; coming into force 1 April 2026; extends to England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
- Regulation 2(2): in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (the national living wage), for '£12.21' substitute '£12.71'.
- Regulation 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b), for '£10.00' substitute '£10.85' — this is the rate for workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21.
- Regulation 2(3)(b) and (c): 16-17 rate and apprentice rate each move from £7.55 to £8.00. Regulation 2(4): accommodation offset from £10.66 to £11.10 per day.
- The Explanatory Note to the same instrument confirms in words: 'Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour… Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour.'
- Corroborated by GOV.UK's rate table (April 2026 row: £12.71 / £10.85 / £8 / £8), the Low Pay Commission report 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (published 1 April 2026), and the LPC press release 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour' (1 April 2026).
- Provenance of the figures: LPC recommendations submitted 27 October 2025, accepted by the Government at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025, given effect by the instrument above. The statutory position is settled.

4. SCOPE AND DEFINITIONS — the four points where HR most often gets this wrong

(a) Age is the determining factor, and the NLW threshold is 21, not 23 or 25. The threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024. Workers aged 20 and under are on the NMW age rates, not the NLW.

(b) This is the statutory National Living Wage. It is not the 'Real Living Wage' (£12.60 / £14.05 London at the last voluntary uprating, set by the Living Wage Foundation and paid voluntarily). Do not substitute one for the other in payroll, contracts, accreditation claims or job adverts.

(c) Apprentices are the main trap. An apprentice is entitled to the Apprentice Rate (£8.00) if they are under 19, or 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. Once an apprentice is 19 or over and has completed the first year, they move to the full rate for their age — so a 21-year-old apprentice past their first year is entitled to £12.71, and a 20-year-old past their first year to £10.85. The £12.71 headline does not apply to every 21+ worker on the payroll.

(d) The rates are hourly minimums for pay reference periods. Salaried staff are not exempt: under the salaried-hours rules, pay must still be at or above the minimum for the hours actually worked. Deductions, required uniform purchases, time spent on training and travel between assignments can all push effective pay below the floor even where the headline hourly rate looks compliant. The accommodation offset is capped at £11.10 per day for April 2026 onward.

5. PAYROLL ACTIONS BEFORE THE FIRST PAY REFERENCE PERIOD BEGINNING ON OR AFTER 1 APRIL 2026

1. Extract every worker aged 21+ currently at or near £12.21 and every worker aged 18-20 at or near £10.00; these are the populations that must move on 1 April.
2. Reconcile age-band assignment against date of birth, not against job title or grade; an employee turning 21 mid-period moves bands on their birthday.
3. Re-run the apprentice check: date of birth, apprenticeship start date, and whether year one is complete.
4. Update the accommodation offset to £11.10/day for any worker in employer-provided living accommodation.
5. Check pay differentials and junior-to-standard differentials for compression — the 8.5% uplift on the 18-20 band is more than double the 4.1% on the NLW, so differentials will narrow.
6. Confirm any salary-sacrifice, deduction or charge-back arrangements do not take effective pay below the floor for the hours worked.
7. Record the rates and the SI reference in the payroll configuration log so the April 2027 uprating is applied against a clean baseline.

6. FORWARD NOTE (out of scope, but it will be asked)

Rates effective 1 April 2027 are already published on GOV.UK: £13.21 (21+), £11.27 (18-20), £8.31 (16-17 and apprentice). They are not the answer to this request and must not be applied before 1 April 2027.

7. VERIFICATION

To re-verify at any point: legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made (regulations 2(2) and 2(3)(a), plus the Explanatory Note) and gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates (April 2026 row). Both must agree; if they ever diverge, the statutory instrument prevails.

# FMCSA Short-Haul Exception (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — Radius and Release Time

## 1. The two answers

| Ask | Answer | Unit | Regulatory basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Radius within which the driver must operate | **150** | **air miles** (172.6 statute miles) | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) |
| 2. Consecutive hours within which the driver must be released from work | **14** | **consecutive hours** | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii) |

A driver qualifies for the exception from the records-of-duty-status requirement only if the driver operates **within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location** and **returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours** (plus the off-duty and carrier-recordkeeping conditions in § 4 below).

## 2. Governing text (verbatim)

49 CFR 395.1(e) — Short-haul operations:

> "(e) Short-haul operations —
> (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
> (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
> (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
> (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
> (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
> (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing:
> (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day;
> (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day;
> (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day;
> (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

FMCSA's own summary of the same provision: *"A driver is exempt from the requirements of § 395.8 and § 395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours. Drivers using the short-haul exception in § 395.1(e)(1) must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours, and stay within a 150 air-mile radius of the work reporting location."* (FMCSA, Summary of Hours of Service Regulations; HOS Visor Card.)

## 3. How the two numbers are measured

**Radius — 150 air miles.**
- "Air mile" means the straight-line (great-circle) distance between the normal work reporting location and the driver's position — not route/road miles. The regulation supplies the conversion itself: 150 air miles = **172.6 statute miles**.
- The circle is centred on the **normal work reporting location**, i.e. the location where the driver reports to and is released from work — not the carrier's terminal, not the shipper, not the driver's residence (unless that is in fact the normal work reporting location).
- The limit is a boundary condition: the driver must remain inside it for the entire tour, not merely start and end inside it. A single excursion beyond 150 air miles defeats the exception for that tour.
- There is **no boundary-crossing allowance** attached to § 395.1(e)(1) (unlike the agricultural exception in § 395.1(k)).

**Release time — 14 consecutive hours.**
- The clock starts when the driver **comes on duty / reports for duty**, and the driver must both (a) **return to the work reporting location** and (b) be **released from work** before the 14th consecutive hour elapses.
- It is a **duty-tour clock, not a driving clock**: it runs continuously through driving, on-duty-not-driving, breaks and any off-duty time taken inside the tour. Off-duty time taken during the tour does **not** extend or pause the 14 hours.
- 14 hours is the outer bound; the exception is lost for any tour in which release occurs at or beyond the 14-hour mark.
- "Released from work" means the carrier has released the driver from duty at the normal work reporting location. A driver who returns to the location but remains on duty (e.g. continues paperwork or is held available) has not been released.
- Driver-salespersons are excluded from the release-time condition by the express carve-out in (e)(1)(ii).

## 4. Conditions precedent — all must hold for the exception to apply

1. Operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location — **ask 1**.
2. Returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours (driver-salespersons excepted) — **ask 2**.
3. Property-carrying: at least **10 consecutive hours off duty** separating each 14 hours on duty. Passenger-carrying: at least **8 consecutive hours** off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
4. The employing motor carrier maintains and retains for **6 months** accurate and true time records of: report-for-duty time each day; total hours on duty each day; release-from-duty time each day; and, for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, total time for the preceding 7 days per § 395.8(j)(2).
5. The driver is not a driver-salesperson (for the release-time condition).

Effect when the conditions are met: the driver is exempt from § 395.8 (record of duty status) and § 395.11; FMCSA states that qualifying property and passenger carriers "are not required to use a RODS or ELD, or take a 30-minute break (§ 395.1(e)(1))." The underlying hours-of-service limits (11-hour driving, 14-hour driving window, 60/70-hour) continue to apply — the exception relieves the paperwork obligation, not the substantive driving limits.

## 5. Frequently confused neighbouring figures — none of these is the answer

| Figure | Where it comes from | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **100 air miles / 12 hours** | The pre-2020 version of § 395.1(e)(1) | **SUPERSEDED.** The 2020 HOS final rule "extends the maximum duty period allowed under the short-haul exception from 12 hours to 14 hours" and "extends the maximum radius of the short-haul exception from a 100 air-mile radius to a 150 air-mile radius." Do not use 100/12. |
| 100 air miles | § 395.1(p), motion-picture production site transportation | A different, narrow exception. Not the short-haul RODS exception. |
| 150 air miles (radius only) | § 395.1(k), agricultural commodities | Same radius figure, different exception with its own terms. |
| 14 hours / 16 hours driving cutoffs | § 395.1(e)(2), the CDL-not-required short-haul variant | See § 6 — a separate paragraph, not a substitute for the 14-hour release answer. |
| 14-hour driving window | § 395.3(a)(2) | The general HOS window; distinct from the 14-consecutive-hour report-to-release tour of (e)(1). |

## 6. Related paragraph to avoid misapplication — § 395.1(e)(2)

A second short-haul provision covers drivers of property-carrying CMVs **for which a CDL is not required** under Part 383. It uses the **same 150 air-mile radius** and requires return to the normal work reporting location **at the end of each duty tour**, but instead of a flat 14-hour release it bars driving:
- after the **14th** hour after coming on duty on **5 days** of any period of 7 consecutive days; and
- after the **16th** hour after coming on duty on **2 days** of any period of 7 consecutive days.

If a driver falls under (e)(2) rather than (e)(1), the radius answer (150 air miles) is unchanged; the release-time answer must be read from (e)(2)(iv), not from (e)(1)(ii). The question as posed — release from work within a set number of consecutive hours — is the (e)(1) formulation, so the answer given is 14.

## 7. Consequence of exceeding either limit

The exception is applied **tour by tour**. If on any day the driver exceeds the 150 air-mile radius, or is not returned and released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception does not apply for that tour and the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day (and, being then a driver required to keep RODS, must use an ELD if otherwise subject to the ELD rule). The carrier's 6-month time records under (e)(1)(iv) are what let the carrier demonstrate the exception was in fact satisfied on the days it was claimed; gaps or inaccuracies in those records undercut the claim for the affected tours.

## 8. Authorities

- 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) — short-haul operations, 150 air-mile radius driver (eCFR, current).
- 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2) — CDL-not-required short-haul variant.
- 49 CFR 395.1(k), 395.1(p) — agricultural and motion-picture exceptions (distinguishing figures).
- 49 CFR 395.3 — underlying hours-of-service limits; 395.8 — record of duty status; 395.11.
- FMCSA, *Hours of Service Drivers Final Rule* (2020 HOS revision: 150 air miles, 14-hour shift).
- FMCSA, *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations*; FMCSA *HOS Visor Card* (short-haul exception restated).

# BasicMed aircraft limits (United States) — current answer

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Ask | Answer | Governing condition |
|---|-----|--------|---------------------|
| 1 | Maximum takeoff weight | **12,500 lb** maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) | Aircraft's maximum *certificated* takeoff weight must not exceed 12,500 lb |
| 2 | Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | **7 occupants** (including required flightcrew) | Aircraft must be authorized under Federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants |
| 3 | Passengers on board | **6 passengers** maximum | The flight may carry not more than 6 passengers |

These are the limits in force **on or after 12 November 2024**, which is the current state of the rule.

## 2. Regulatory basis and effective date

- **Statute:** Section 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (PL 114-190), as amended by **Section 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63)**, which defines a "covered aircraft" and expands the BasicMed aircraft conditions.
- **Implementing rule:** Final rule, RIN 2120-AM06, Docket FAA-2024-2580, Federal Register doc. 2024-26935, published **18 November 2024**. Its own summary states it amends the regulations "to align aircraft conditions and limitations with the term 'covered aircraft' as defined in section 2307(j) of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 to increase the number of allowable passengers from 5 to 6, increase the number of occupants from 6 to 7, and increase the maximum takeoff weight from 6,000 pounds to 12,500 pounds, while excluding certain transport category rotorcraft."
- **Operative date for the aircraft limits:** **12 November 2024.** FAA Notice **N 8000.386** (dated 14 November 2024) states: "Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, the aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and the aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board."
- **Regulatory home:** 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) (BasicMed operating conditions), read with 14 CFR part 68; for experimental aircraft the occupant cap also appears at 14 CFR 91.319(j).
- **Corroboration:** The FAA BasicMed page currently lists, under Aircraft Requirements, "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants" and "Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds," and under Operating Requirements, "Carries not more than six passengers." The FAA newsroom release of 15 November 2024 ("FAA Updates BasicMed Program") states the same three numbers.

## 3. Precision on each term

**Maximum takeoff weight (ask 1).** This is the aircraft's **maximum certificated takeoff weight** — the number in the type certificate data sheet (TCDS) or other design approval — not the actual weight of the aircraft on a given flight. An aircraft with a certificated MTOW above 12,500 lb does not qualify, even if it is flown light. Conversely, if an aircraft certificated above the ceiling is altered so that its maximum certificated takeoff weight is at or below 12,500 lb (via STC or amended TC), it can qualify; AC 68-1A §5.1.2 sets out this alteration logic for the original 6,000 lb ceiling, and the same reasoning applies to the current 12,500 lb ceiling.

**Occupants authorized (ask 2).** This is the number of occupants the **aircraft is authorized to carry under Federal law** — its design approval (TC, STC, or amended TC) — not the number of seats installed and not the number of people actually on board. AC 68-1A §5.1.2: "the aircraft's design approval would authorize the number of occupants the aircraft may carry and would contain the maximum certificated takeoff weight… So long as an aircraft's design approval (i.e., TC, STC, or ATC) authorizes the aircraft to carry no more than six occupants, that aircraft would meet the requirements." The 2017 Safety Briefing makes the practical point with the pre-expansion number: variants certificated to carry more than the ceiling do not qualify "even if they only have six seats installed." With the current ceiling, read "seven" wherever that guidance says "six." For **experimental** aircraft, which have no type certificate, the occupant cap is imposed directly by 14 CFR 91.319(j) (AC 68-1A §5.1.3 addressed the six-occupant version of that section; the 2024 final rule conformed the regulations to the new covered-aircraft definition, so confirm the amended text of § 91.319(j) before relying on it for a specific experimental aircraft).

**Passengers on board (ask 3).** This is a limit on the **flight**, not on the aircraft's paper capacity: no more than **6 passengers**. Because "occupants" includes required flightcrew, the passenger cap is what actually binds as crew size grows.

## 4. How the two occupancy numbers interact (worked cases)

Occupants = flightcrew + passengers. The aircraft may be *authorized* for up to 7; the flight may *carry* up to 6 passengers.

| Crew required/aboard | Max passengers permitted | Total occupants | Within 7-occupant authorization? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 pilot | 6 | 7 | Yes (at the limit) |
| 2 pilots | 5 | 7 | Yes (at the limit) |
| 1 pilot + 1 non-required crew/safety pilot | 5 | 7 | Yes |

A 7-occupant-authorized aircraft flown single-pilot can carry 6 passengers; the same aircraft flown with two pilots can carry 5 passengers. Both satisfy both conditions. An aircraft authorized for 8 or more occupants fails the aircraft condition regardless of how many people are aboard.

## 5. Superseded figures — do not use

The pre-12 November 2024 limits were **6,000 lb MTOW, 6 occupants authorized, 5 passengers**. These still appear in older but widely circulated documents and must not be quoted as current:

- **AC 68-1A** (3 May 2017), §3.2: "Fly with no more than five passengers… maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than 6,000 lbs… authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants."
- **FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017**, "The BasicMed Issue": "any aircraft with a maximum take-off weight of 6,000 pounds or less, and certified to carry not more than six occupants."
- **Notice N 8000.386** itself lists the 6,000 lb / 6 / 5 set as the conditions applicable *before* 12 November 2024, alongside the new set.

If a document you are relying on says 6,000 lb, it predates the expansion.

## 6. Verification procedure (for a specific aircraft)

1. Identify the make/model/serial number and the applicable **design approval**: TC, STC, or amended TC; for experimental, the operating limitations and 14 CFR 91.319(j).
2. Pull the **TCDS** (FAA website) or the STC/ATC paperwork and read (a) maximum certificated takeoff weight and (b) approved occupant capacity.
3. Test: MTOW ≤ 12,500 lb **and** authorized occupants ≤ 7 **and** aircraft is not a transport category rotorcraft excluded from the expansion.
4. At dispatch, test: passengers aboard ≤ 6 and total occupants ≤ 7.
5. Record the basis (TCDS revision date / STC number) in the flight or training records.

## 7. Caveats

- **Transport category rotorcraft.** The 2024 expansion excludes certain transport category rotorcraft. For a transport category helicopter, do not assume the 12,500 lb / 7-occupant figures apply; verify against the amended rule text and the covered-aircraft definition before flight.
- **Other BasicMed conditions are unchanged and not part of this answer.** BasicMed flight operations remain limited to VFR or IFR, within the United States (or another country in which BasicMed is authorized), at or below 18,000 ft MSL, at an indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots, and not for compensation or hire. The whole flight must comply — a BasicMed pilot cannot act as PIC for any portion of a flight that exceeds these limits, even if another pilot aboard holds a medical certificate.
- **Pilot-side eligibility is separate.** Holding a valid U.S. driver's license, having held an FAA medical certificate at any point after 14 July 2006, a current CMEC from a state-licensed physician, and a completed BasicMed online course are prerequisites independent of the three aircraft numbers above.
- **Currency of this answer.** Figures are as of the sources fetched 17 November 2026, reflecting the rule effective 18 November 2024 and the 12 November 2024 statutory trigger. Any later rulemaking or new FAA guidance would supersede them; re-check 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) and the FAA BasicMed page before relying on this in a checkride, insurance, or enforcement context.

# Hours of service for the driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach) — US federal rules

**Governing provision:** 49 CFR 395.5, *Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles* (49 CFR Part 395, Subpart A), read '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1.' Quoted text below is from the current eCFR text of § 395.5 and the 2025 printed CFR (Title 49, Vol. 5), both fetched for this task.

## 0. Applicability check (do this first — everything below depends on it)

Part 395 splits into two parallel rule sets: § 395.3 for **property**-carrying CMVs and § 395.5 for **passenger**-carrying CMVs. The limits are not interchangeable, so confirm the vehicle is passenger-carrying before applying any number here.

A motorcoach is a passenger-carrying CMV: 49 CFR 390.5 defines a CMV as a self-propelled or towed motor vehicle used on a highway in interstate commerce to transport passengers or property when the vehicle, among other tests, '(2) Is designed or used to transport more than 8 passengers (including the driver) for compensation' or has a GVWR/GCWR of 10,001 lb or more. A motorcoach carrying passengers for compensation meets that test. If the operation is instead a property-carrying CMV (e.g., a courier van, or a bus converted to freight), § 395.3 applies and the numbers are 11 / 10 / 14 — **not** the numbers below.

## 1. The three limits (the answers)

### Ask 1 — Maximum driving: **10 hours**
§ 395.5(a)(1): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV '[m]ore than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'

That is 10 hours of *driving time* accumulated in the on-duty period that begins at the end of the 8 consecutive hours off duty. It is not 10 hours of on-duty time, and it is not extendable by on-duty non-driving work.

### Ask 2 — Required consecutive off duty: **8 hours**
Same subsection: the 10-hour driving allowance is measured 'following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' The 8 hours must be **consecutive** and must be **off duty** (not on duty, not driving). This is the sharpest difference from the property-carrying rule, which requires 10 consecutive hours off duty (§ 395.3(a)(1)). A motorcoach driver does **not** need 10 consecutive hours under the federal passenger rule.

Note on sleeper berths: under § 395.2, sleeper-berth time is not 'on-duty time' (on-duty time excludes sleeper-berth periods), so sleeper-berth time counts toward the 8 consecutive hours off duty for a passenger-carrying driver. Unlike the property rule, § 395.5 contains **no** split sleeper-berth provision and § 395.1(g)'s sleeper-berth pairing rules are written for property-carrying drivers — do not try to run a 7/3 or 8/2 split against the passenger 8-hour requirement. (Confidence: high on the text; the sleeper-berth-counts-as-off-duty point is settled practice, but confirm with counsel if it is load-bearing for a specific schedule.)

### Ask 3 — On-duty ceiling for driving: **15 hours**
§ 395.5(a)(2): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, 'for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'

Driving is prohibited once the driver has been on duty 15 hours measured from the end of the last 8 consecutive hours off duty. The 15-hour clock is an **on-duty** clock, not a driving clock: all on-duty non-driving time (pre-trip inspection, loading, waiting at the terminal, dispatch, paperwork) counts against it. The 15-hour window and the 10-hour driving allowance run concurrently — the driver's 10 driving hours must be completed inside the same 15-hour on-duty window.

## 2. Cumulative weekly limits (a second, independent driving prohibition)

§ 395.5(b) bars driving 'for any period after—'
- **(b)(1)** '[h]aving been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week'; or
- **(b)(2)** '[h]aving been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.'

These are rolling multi-day totals, not a daily figure, so they are reported here rather than as the answer to ask 3. Which one applies is a property of the **carrier's operating schedule**, not the driver's preference: a carrier that runs CMVs every day of the week is on the 70/8 cycle; one that does not is on the 60/7 cycle. A driver used by more than one carrier must count on-duty time for all of them (§ 395.5(b): 'regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services').

Practical effect: a driver may be well inside the 10-hour and 15-hour limits and still be prohibited from driving because the 60- or 70-hour total is exhausted. Conversely, hitting 60/70 bars **driving**; it does not by its terms bar remaining on duty on non-driving tasks, though the time still accrues to the cycle.

**No 34-hour restart.** The § 395.3(c) restart is a property-carrying provision. § 395.5 has no restart paragraph. A passenger-carrying driver regains driving eligibility only when enough off-duty time has passed that the prior on-duty hours roll out of the 7- or 8-day window.

## 3. What does not apply (importing these would give wrong numbers)

| Rule | Applies to | Status for passenger-carrying |
|---|---|---|
| 11-hour driving limit, § 395.3(a)(1) | Property | Does not apply — use 10 (§ 395.5(a)(1)) |
| 14-hour driving window, § 395.3(a)(2) | Property | Does not apply — use the 15-hour **on-duty** limit (§ 395.5(a)(2)) |
| 10 consecutive hours off duty, § 395.3(a)(1) | Property | Does not apply — 8 consecutive hours (§ 395.5(a)(1)) |
| 34-hour restart, § 395.3(c) | Property | Does not apply |
| Split sleeper berth, § 395.1(g) | Property | Does not apply — take the 8 hours in one block |
| Short-haul exemption, § 395.1(e) | Property (CDL and non-CDL) | Does not apply to passenger-carrying operations |

## 4. Exceptions that could move the numbers — flag, don't silently apply

- **Adverse driving conditions, § 395.1(b)(1).** A driver who encounters adverse driving conditions (as defined in § 395.2) 'may drive and be permitted or required to drive a commercial motor vehicle for the period of time needed to complete the run.' This relieves the **driving-time** limit. Because § 395.5(a)(2) is an **on-duty** limit, the exception should not be read to extend the 15-hour on-duty prohibition — driving after the 15th on-duty hour remains a violation. Treat this as the conservative reading and confirm before relying on any extension of the 15-hour clock. (Confidence: moderate-high; this is an interpretation point, not quoted text.)
- **State law.** Part 395 governs CMVs in **interstate** commerce. A state may impose stricter hours-of-service requirements, and purely **intrastate** motorcoach operations are governed by the state's own HOS rules (which must be compatible with the federal rules under the MCSAP framework, 49 CFR Part 350). If the operation never crosses a state line, verify the state rule before using these numbers.
- **Statutory/regulatory exemptions, § 395.1 generally.** § 395.5 is expressly '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1.' If any exemption (e.g., a specific statutory exemption for a particular operation) is claimed, the numbers above are displaced to that extent.
- **Company policy.** Carrier policy may be stricter than the legal minimum; it cannot be looser.

## 5. Worked example (checking the arithmetic against all three limits)

Driver comes off 8 consecutive hours off duty at 06:00. On duty at 06:00.

- 15-hour on-duty ceiling: 06:00 + 15 h = **21:00**. No driving at or after 21:00.
- 10-hour driving allowance: at most **10:00** of the 15 hours may be driving; the other 5 hours (or more) must be on-duty non-driving or off duty.
- Suppose the driver drives 4 h, is on duty non-driving 1 h, drives 4 h, takes 1 h off duty, drives 2 h → 10 h driving reached at 18:00, 12 h on duty. Driving is over: the 10-hour limit is exhausted at 18:00 even though the 15-hour window runs to 21:00. Additional on-duty non-driving work may continue to 21:00, but not driving.
- Suppose instead the driver's driving is light: 6 h driving but 15 h on duty (long loading/waiting). Driving stops at 21:00 regardless of the 4 unused driving hours.
- Separately test the cycle: if the carrier runs CMVs every day and the driver already has 68 on-duty hours in the last 8 days, the driver may add at most 2 more on-duty hours before the § 395.5(b)(2) driving prohibition attaches, regardless of the daily clocks.

## 6. Recordkeeping context

Compliance with all three limits is evidenced by the driver's record of duty status under § 395.8 (24-hour duty-status grid, with the ELD requirements of Part 395 Subpart B for drivers subject to the ELD rule). Carriers must retain records of duty status and supporting documents for at least 6 months (§ 395.8(k)(1)). When a driver is used by more than one carrier, the driver must furnish each carrier a copy of the record of duty status covering all duty time in the 24-hour period, and a carrier using a driver for the first time or intermittently must obtain a signed statement of the driver's total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty (§ 395.8(j)). Those statements are how the 60/70-hour total is verified across carriers.

## 7. Verification of every stated number against every stated threshold

| Stated value | Source | Cross-check |
|---|---|---|
| 10 h driving | § 395.5(a)(1) | 10 ≤ 15 (on-duty ceiling) — consistent; driving cannot outlast the window |
| 8 h consecutive off duty | § 395.5(a)(1) | 8 < 10 (property rule) — correct direction for passenger; 8 h resets both the 10-h and 15-h clocks, so no residual clock conflicts |
| 15 h on duty | § 395.5(a)(2) | Measured from end of the same 8 consecutive hours off duty as the 10-h limit — single shared anchor, no dual-anchor inconsistency |
| 60 h / 7 days | § 395.5(b)(1) | Applies only when carrier does not operate CMVs every day; mutually exclusive with (b)(2) |
| 70 h / 8 days | § 395.5(b)(2) | Applies only when carrier operates CMVs every day; mutually exclusive with (b)(1) |
| No 34-h restart | § 395.5 text contains no restart; § 395.3(c) is property-only | Does not create a fourth number that could contradict the three answers |

No stated value exceeds or contradicts another stated limit.

## 8. One-line answer for the driver

**Drive no more than 10 hours, after at least 8 consecutive hours off duty, and never after you have been on duty 15 hours — and in any case never after 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day) or 70 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day).**
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.5 and 15 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"
