# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Answer

| Item | Value | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum rest after a scheduled duty period of **14 hours or less** | **9 consecutive hours** (scheduled rest period) | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| Lowest rest to which that may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

Both figures are *consecutive* hours. There is no authority in 135.273 to go below 8 consecutive hours for this duty-period band.

## 2. Governing text (verbatim, 14 CFR 135.273, current e-CFR / 2026 CFR edition)

**135.273(a) — definitions:**

> **Duty period** means the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder. The time is calculated using either Coordinated Universal Time or local time to reflect the total elapsed time.
>
> **Flight attendant** means an individual, other than a flight crewmember, who is assigned by the certificate holder, in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or in addition to that minimum complement, to duty in an aircraft during flight time and whose duties include but are not necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities.
>
> **Rest period** means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.

**135.273(b) — duty period limitations and rest requirements:**

> (b) Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section, a certificate holder may assign a duty period to a flight attendant only when the applicable duty period limitations and rest requirements of this paragraph are met.
>
> (1) Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours.
>
> (2) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> (3) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

**135.273(b)(10), (11) — absolute bars:**

> (10) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section.
>
> (11) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period.

**135.261(e) — scope (why an on-demand charter holder is covered):**

> (e) Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part.

Note the contrast with 135.261(b)–(d): the flight crewmember sections (135.265/267/269) apply selectively by operation type, but 135.273 applies to **all** Part 135 operations. No election, ops-spec amendment, or scheduled-service finding is needed to make the flight attendant rule apply.

## 3. The five conditions on the reduction to 8 hours

A reduction from 9 to 8 consecutive hours is lawful only if **all** of the following are satisfied:

1. **Floor.** The rest is not less than 8 consecutive hours. (b)(3)
2. **Compensatory rest.** The flight attendant is given a *subsequent* rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours**. (b)(3)
3. **Clock deadline measured from the START of the reduced rest.** That subsequent rest must be *scheduled to begin* no later than **24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** — not 24 hours after its end, and not 24 hours after the duty period ended. (b)(3)
4. **Placement.** Both the reduced rest and the subsequent rest must fall between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. (b)(2), (b)(3)
5. **No work during rest.** No duty of any kind may be assigned during either rest period; a rest period is "free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise" — no standby/reserve availability, no call-in, no administrative or training duty. (b)(11), (a)

Failure of condition 2, 3, or 4 means the rest was not reducible: the flight attendant was entitled to the full 9 consecutive hours, and assigning duty off an 8-hour rest is a violation of (b)(2) and (b)(10).

## 4. Worked timeline (verification of the arithmetic)

Scheduled duty period 06:00–20:00 local, 14.0 hours (at the top of the "14 hours or less" band).

**Baseline (no reduction):** rest begins at release, 20:00. 9 consecutive hours → duty may not be assigned before **05:00** the next day.

**Reduced:** rest begins 20:00, 8 consecutive hours → earliest assignment **04:00** the next day. Because reduced rest began at 20:00, the compensatory 10-hour rest must **begin no later than 20:00 the following day**. Example that complies: next duty period 04:00–14:00 (10.0 hours), release 14:00, subsequent rest 14:00→00:00 = 10.0 consecutive hours, which begins 14:00, i.e., 18 hours after the 20:00 start of the reduced rest (≤ 24). Complies.

Example that fails: next duty 04:00–22:00, release 22:00. Subsequent rest would begin 22:00, which is 26 hours after the 20:00 start of the reduced rest — outside the 24-hour window. The 8-hour reduction was therefore not available; the crewmember needed 9 hours and could not be assigned at 04:00.

## 5. Point that is most often gotten wrong

**135.273(b)(9) does not apply to this reduction.** That paragraph reads:

> (9) Notwithstanding paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, if a certificate holder elects to reduce the rest period to 10 hours as authorized by paragraph (b)(8) of this section, the certificate holder may not schedule a flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest period.

By its terms it is triggered only by a **10-hour** reduction under **(b)(8)**, which is the rest attaching to *extended* duty periods of more than 14 (up to 20) hours under (b)(4)–(b)(6). It imposes no 14-hour next-duty cap on an 8-hour reduction under (b)(3). Do not import it; doing so would ground aircraft unnecessarily. Conversely, do not import the (b)(3) 10-hour compensatory-rest condition into a (b)(8) 10-hour reduction — (b)(8) requires 14 consecutive hours of subsequent rest.

## 6. Context: the longer-duty branches (for completeness, not part of the answer)

- (b)(4): scheduled duty >14 but ≤16 hours, permitted if at least **one** additional flight attendant beyond the ops-spec minimum is assigned.
- (b)(5): >16 but ≤18 hours, at least **two** additional flight attendants.
- (b)(6): >18 but ≤20 hours, at least **three** additional flight attendants, and the duty period must include one or more flights landing or taking off outside the 48 contiguous states and D.C.
- (b)(7): a flight attendant scheduled to >14 but ≤20 hours must get **12 consecutive hours** of scheduled rest.
- (b)(8): that 12 hours may be scheduled or reduced to **10 consecutive hours** if followed by at least **14 consecutive hours** of subsequent rest beginning no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest; and (b)(9) then caps the next duty period at 14 hours in the following 24.

Summary of the bands: ≤14 h duty → 9 h rest, reducible to 8 h (10 h makeup). >14–20 h duty → 12 h rest, reducible to 10 h (14 h makeup, plus the 14-hour next-duty cap).

## 7. Two caveats the operator must clear before applying the 9/8 answer

**(a) 135.273(c) alternative election.** A certificate holder may, instead of (b), apply the *flight crewmember* flight time/duty/rest rules to its flight attendants, provided it establishes written procedures that apply to all flight attendants in its operation, incorporate the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (on-board rest facilities not required), add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flight crewmember above the type-certificate minimum, and are **approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications**. If — and only if — this operator holds such approved procedures, the answer is not 9/8 but the flight-crewmember table of 135.265(b)/(c): 9 hours for <8 h scheduled flight time, 10 hours for 8 to <9 h, 11 hours for ≥9 h, reducible respectively to 8, 8, and 9 hours with compensating 10/11/12-hour rest beginning within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest. **Action: pull the ops specs and confirm no 135.273(c) election is in effect.** Absent that, 9/8 governs.

**(b) Whether a flight attendant is assigned at all.** 135.273 governs only individuals meeting the (a) definition — assigned per the ops-spec minimum crew complement or in addition to it, with cabin-safety duties. If a given flight is not required to and does not carry a flight attendant, the rule has no subject. The question presumes one is assigned; if the operator's seating configuration/ops specs never require one, say so rather than applying 9/8 to a crewmember who is not a "flight attendant."

Neither caveat makes the question unanswerable — the Part 135 flight attendant rule is 9 → 8 — but both change the number if present, so they belong in the compliance file.

## 8. Assumptions and limits of this answer

- Source is the current e-CFR text of 135.273 and the 2026 CFR (GovInfo) edition of Part 135, retrieved 2026-11-17. The section has been stable since the 1994 amendments (Amdt. 135-52); still, re-verify against e-CFR at the time of any enforcement-sensitive use, and check for any FAA-issued exemption, letter of interpretation, or ops-spec deviation held by this specific certificate holder.
- This is the **regulatory floor**. A collective bargaining agreement or company manual may impose more rest; the more restrictive term controls as a matter of contract/policy, not regulation.
- The rest table is keyed to the **scheduled** duty period. The regulation contains no separate rest table keyed to an actual duty period that overruns its schedule. Where actual duty exceeds the schedule, the rest is still computed from actual release (a rest period cannot begin before release, since the crewmember is not yet free of responsibility), but whether an overrun past 14 hours pulls the flight into the (b)(4)–(b)(7) regime is a question of how the assignment was scheduled and is not resolved by the text alone — treat an overrun past 14 hours conservatively (12 hours of rest) and obtain FSDO/legal confirmation. This is the one point in the answer that is interpretive rather than textual.
- Time basis: the holder must use either UTC or local time consistently to reflect total elapsed time (135.273(a), "Duty period"). Document which basis the schedule uses.

## 9. Compliance checklist for the scheduling/dispatch system

1. Compute scheduled duty period length (report to release).
2. If ≤14.0 h → required rest = 9 consecutive hours, measured from actual release.
3. To use 8 hours, flag the pairing and verify in the system: (i) 8 ≥ rest ≥ 8; (ii) a subsequent rest block ≥10 consecutive hours exists; (iii) that block begins ≤ (start of reduced rest + 24:00); (iv) both blocks lie between end of the scheduled duty period and start of the subsequent duty period.
4. Hard-block any assignment during a required rest period (b)(11); do not allow reserve/standby or administrative duty to be coded into a rest block.
5. If any condition in step 3 fails, restore the rest to 9 hours and re-solve the pairing.
6. Confirm the ops specs contain no 135.273(c) election before deploying the 9/8 logic as the rule engine's default.

# HTTP/2: current specification and what it obsoletes

## Answer

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, Standards Track (Proposed Standard), IETF HTTPBIS working group; editors M. Thomson and C. Benfield |
| 2 | RFCs that RFC 9113 obsoletes | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** (exactly two) |

Source of record: RFC Editor subject page for HTTP/2 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/), RFC Editor info page for RFC 9113 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113), IETF Datatracker doc pages for RFC 9113 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/) and RFC 7540 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7540/), and the HTTPWG published copy of the RFC (https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html). All fetched 2026-11-17T05:46:51Z.

---

## 1. The current specification: RFC 9113

RFC 9113, *HTTP/2*, was published June 2022 on the IETF Standards Track as a Proposed Standard. It is the document the RFC Editor files under the HTTP/2 subject area as the current entry, and the same page marks its two predecessors as obsoleted by it.

Evidence, quoted from the fetched pages:

- RFC 9113 header block (httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html): `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`, `Category: Standards Track`, `June 2022`, title `HTTP/2`.
- RFC 9113 abstract: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
- RFC Editor HTTP/2 subject page, newest-first: "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 — Proposed Standard — M. Thomson, C. Benfield — June 2022 — IETF publication".
- Same page, RFC 7540 entry: "Obsoleted by RFC 9113". Same page, RFC 8740 entry: "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".
- Datatracker rfc9113 page repeats the abstract sentence verbatim.

Two clarifications a reader will otherwise get wrong:

- **It is a Proposed Standard, not an Internet Standard.** RFC 9113's Status of This Memo reads "This is an Internet Standards Track document." That is a track, not a maturity level of Internet Standard. Do not describe HTTP/2 as an Internet Standard.
- **httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html is the same document, not a competing spec.** It is the HTTP Working Group's HTML rendering of RFC 9113. Cite it as a rendering of RFC 9113, never as an alternative to it.

---

## 2. What RFC 9113 obsoletes: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740

The authoritative field is the `Obsoletes` header, which names two documents:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title | Publication | Authors | Why it is in the list |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)* | May 2015, Proposed Standard | M. Belshe, R. Peon, M. Thomson (ed.) | It was the original HTTP/2 specification; RFC 9113 is its full revision. |
| **RFC 8740** | *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2* | February 2020, Proposed Standard | D. Benjamin | It was a stand-alone addendum to RFC 7540; RFC 9113 folds TLS 1.3 usage into the main text, so the addendum is absorbed rather than left dangling. |

RFC 9113's own Appendix B states this directly: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."

**The obsoleted set is exactly {RFC 7540, RFC 8740}. Answering "RFC 7540" alone is incomplete and is the most common error on this question.**

---

## 3. Obsoletes vs Updates — the distinction that must not be collapsed

These are different relations and RFC 9113's header uses only the first for these two documents:

```
RFC 7540  (HTTP/2, 2015) ──obsoleted by──► RFC 9113
RFC 8740  (TLS 1.3 w/ HTTP/2, 2020) ──obsoleted by──► RFC 9113
         └── RFC 8740 itself "updates RFC 7540" (an earlier, separate edge)
```

- RFC 8740's abstract, per the RFC Editor subject page: "This document updates RFC 7540 by forbidding TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication..." — so 8740 was an *Updates* document in 2020, and became an *Obsoleted* document in 2022. Both statements are true of different time periods; neither contradicts the other.
- RFC 9113's captured header shows an `Obsoletes` field and no `Updates` field. That is an observation about the fetched header block; if the Updates relation matters for a downstream registry, confirm against https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 rather than inferring from this memo.

---

## 4. What RFC 9113 does NOT obsolete (guard against over-listing)

The following RFCs appear on the RFC Editor HTTP/2 subject page with no "Obsoleted by" marker and remain in force. They must not be added to the answer to ask 2:

| RFC | Title | Relation to RFC 9113 |
|---|---|---|
| RFC 7541 | HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2 | Still current; RFC 9113 references it for field compression. Not obsoleted. |
| RFC 8441 | Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2 | Still current. Not obsoleted. |
| RFC 8336 | The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame | Still current. Not obsoleted. |

Context only, not part of either answer: RFC 9218 (*Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP*) is *recommended* by RFC 9113 §5.3.2 and Appendix B in place of the deprecated RFC 7540 priority scheme; RFC 9113 does not obsolete it, and the RFC 7540 priority *signalling semantics* are deprecated but the frame/field formats are retained for interoperability.

---

## 5. Reproducible verification procedure

Anyone re-checking this should run the following and expect the stated result. It takes about two minutes.

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/ with sort = "Newest first".
   - Expect the first entry to be RFC 9113, June 2022, Proposed Standard.
   - Expect the RFC 7540 and RFC 8740 entries each to carry the badge "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".
   - Expect no other entry on the page to carry an "Obsoleted by RFC 9113" badge.
2. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 and read the header block.
   - Expect `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740` — two values, comma-separated.
   - Expect `Category: Standards Track` and a June 2022 date.
3. Open https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ and read the abstract.
   - Expect the sentence "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
4. Cross-check the reverse direction on https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7540/.
   - Expect the 2015 document to be flagged as obsoleted by RFC 9113, confirming the edge is recorded on both ends.
5. Record the lookup date with the answer. RFC status is time-varying; an answer without a lookup date is not verifiable later.

Consistency check on the final answer: the obsoleted list must contain exactly the two identifiers in the `Obsoletes` header, no more and no fewer. If a lookup returns anything other than {7540, 8740}, the header and the subject page disagree and the header wins.

---

## 6. Assumptions made (stated, not hidden)

1. **"Current" = the most recently published IETF Standards Track RFC for HTTP/2 as of the lookup date 2026-11-17.** It does not mean "the version a particular product implements," and it does not mean a working-copy draft.
2. **Internet-Drafts are excluded.** A draft that may eventually supersede RFC 9113 does not make RFC 9113 non-current; only publication of a successor RFC does.
3. **Errata are excluded from the answer.** Errata correct text within RFC 9113; they do not change its number and do not obsolete it. Consult https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/ for the errata list if the corrected text matters.
4. **The obsoleted list is taken from the `Obsoletes` header**, i.e. the direct predecessors named by RFC 9113, not a transitive closure over the whole historical HTTP/2 document lineage.
5. **RFC 9113 has not been superseded as of 2026-11-17** per the fetched RFC Editor and Datatracker records. If this memo is reused later, re-run §5 first.

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 113 on httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html and 540 on datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7540. The first reads: "Information about the current status of this document, any errata, and how to provide feedback on it may be obtained at https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113."

UK STATUTORY MINIMUM WAGE RATES EFFECTIVE 1 APRIL 2026

ANSWERS
1. National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over): £12.71 per hour.
2. National Minimum Wage, 18-20 Year Old Rate (workers aged 18, 19 or 20): £10.85 per hour.

Both are in pounds sterling, per hour, at the officially published precision (nearest penny). Both took effect on 1 April 2026 and apply UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) — the instrument extends to all four nations and there is no regional or sector variation in the statutory rate.

LEGAL BASIS
The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/357), made under ss.1(3), 2(1), (2)(d) and (5), 3(2)(b) and 51(1)(a) of the National Minimum Wage Act 1998, laid in draft under s.51(5) and approved by resolution of each House, coming into force 1 April 2026. They amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (S.I. 2015/621):
- reg. 2(2): reg. 4 (the national living wage) — '£12.21' replaced by '£12.71'.
- reg. 2(3)(a): reg. 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21) — '£10.00' replaced by '£10.85'.
- reg. 2(3)(b): reg. 4A(1)(c) (under 18) — '£7.55' replaced by '£8.00'.
- reg. 2(3)(c): reg. 4A(1)(d) (apprentice rate) — '£7.55' replaced by '£8.00'.
- reg. 2(4): reg. 16(1) (accommodation offset) — '£10.66' replaced by '£11.10' per day.

CORROBORATION
- Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026': table of rates to apply from 1 April 2026 — NLW (21 and over) £12.71 (+£0.50, 4.1%); 18-20 Year Old Rate £10.85 (+£0.85, 8.5%); 16-17 Year Old Rate £8.00 (+£0.45, 6.0%); Apprentice Rate £8.00 (+£0.45, 6.0%); Accommodation Offset £11.10 (+£0.44, 4.1%).
- Low Pay Commission press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', published 1 April 2026: rates 'came into force from 1 April 2026'. Notes the LPC's recommendations were submitted 27 October 2025 and accepted in full by the Government at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.
- GOV.UK 'National Minimum Wage rates' page: April 2026 row — 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; under 18 £8; apprentice £8. The same page also carries an April 2027 row (£13.21 / £11.27 / £8.31 / £8.31), which is a forward rate and is NOT the answer to either question.
- ONS, 'Low and high pay in the UK: 2026' (ASHE): 'On the ASHE reference date in April 2026, the NMW and NLW rates were: £12.71 for employees aged 21 years and over; £10.85 for employees aged 18 to 20 years; £8 for employees aged 16 to 17 years; £8 for apprentices...'.

ARITHMETIC CHECK
12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71; 0.50 / 12.21 = 4.09% (published 4.1%).
10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85; 0.85 / 10.00 = 8.5% (published 8.5%).
10.85 / 12.71 = 85.4%, consistent with the 18-20 rate as a proportion of the adult rate.
Accommodation offset: 10.66 + 0.44 = 11.10; 0.44 / 10.66 = 4.13% (published 4.1%).
16-17 and apprentice: 7.55 + 0.45 = 8.00; 0.45 / 7.55 = 5.96% (published 6.0%).
All stated figures agree with one another and with the published percentage increases.

SCOPE NOTES FOR USE
- 'From April 2026' is read as the rate taking effect on 1 April 2026 (the standard annual uprating date), not a rate announced in April 2026. In practice the figures were announced earlier — LPC advice 27 October 2025, accepted at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025 — so both readings converge on the same numbers.
- 'National Living Wage' here means the statutory NLW set under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998. It is not the Living Wage Foundation's voluntary 'Real Living Wage', which ONS records as £13.45 per hour outside London and £14.80 per hour in London in April 2026. Do not substitute those figures.
- Age bands in force for 2026/27: NLW for 21 and over; 18-20 Year Old Rate for 18, 19 and 20 year olds; 16-17 Year Old Rate for those above school leaving age but under 18; Apprentice Rate for apprentices under 19, or 19 and over in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to the NLW (£12.71), not the apprentice rate.
- The rate that governs compliance is the one in force on the date the work is performed, not the date pay is processed. Work performed on or before 31 March 2026 is governed by the 2025/26 rates (NLW £12.21; 18-20 £10.00; under 18 £7.55; apprentice £7.55; accommodation offset £10.66). Work performed on or after 1 April 2026 is governed by the rates above. Any pay period straddling 1 April 2026 must be apportioned.
- The 18-20 Year Old Rate remains in force for 2026/27. The LPC has noted the Government's stated policy of eventually removing that band, but that has no effect on the £10.85 rate applicable from 1 April 2026.
- April 2027 rates (£13.21 for 21 and over; £11.27 for 18-20) are already published and are shown here only to distinguish them from the requested 2026 figures.

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — RADIUS AND RELEASE-TIME LIMITS

ANSWERS
1. Radius: 150 air miles (the regulation states the equivalent as 172.6 statute miles) from the normal work reporting location.
2. Release: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

CONTROLLING TEXT
49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), '150 air-mile radius driver':
  'A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
   (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
   (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
   (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
   (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.'
Source: eCFR current 49 CFR 395.1 (fetched 2026-11-17); identical text in GovInfo CFR-2024-title49-vol5-sec395-1; FMCSA 'Summary of Hours of Service Regulations' restates: 'the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours... must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours.'

HOW TO MEASURE AND APPLY
- Radius is measured in AIR MILES, not road/statute miles. 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles (conversion factor 1.15078). Measuring by odometer road distance understates the permitted area and is the most common compliance error on this point. The radius is centered on the normal work reporting location — the location where the driver reports to and is released from work — not on the driver's residence or the carrier's terminal if those differ.
- The 14-hour clock runs from the time the driver comes on duty; the driver must both (a) physically return to the normal work reporting location and (b) be released from work there, by hour 14. This is a duty-period limit, not merely a driving limit: it is not extended by off-duty time taken during the day.
- Operation type does not change either answer. 395.1(e)(1) applies the same 150-air-mile radius and the same 14-consecutive-hour release to property-carrying and passenger-carrying drivers; the property/passenger distinction appears only in (e)(1)(iii) — 10 consecutive hours off-duty for property-carrying, 8 for passenger-carrying.
- Scope of relief: the exception relieves the driver of the records-of-duty-status requirement (395.8) and the ELD requirement (395.11). It does not repeal the underlying driving/on-duty limits of 395.3, except to the extent 395.1(e)(1) is the operative provision; the driver must still comply with the 11-hour driving and 60/70-hour limits and remains subject to the 30-minute break provision.
- The carrier must still keep accurate and true time records for 6 months showing report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and the preceding 7 days' total time for newly or intermittently used drivers.

RELATED VARIANT — DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE ANSWER ABOVE
- 395.1(e)(2) (property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL): same 150 air-mile radius, but the release structure differs — the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour, and may not drive after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days nor after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7. Drivers using (e)(2) are ineligible for (e)(1).
- 395.1(p) (motion picture production sites): 100 air-mile radius — a different, narrower exception.

VERSION CONTROL
These values reflect the HOS final rule published June 1, 2020, mandatory compliance September 29, 2020, which expanded the short-haul exception from 100 air miles to 150 air miles and from 12 hours to 14 hours. A pre-September 29, 2020 fact pattern would be governed by the older 100-air-mile / 12-hour figures; the current-regulation values stated above are the correct answers to this request.

NON-FEDERAL CAVEAT
These are the FMCSA interstate figures. A state intrastate hours-of-service regime may set a different radius or release time; if the driver's operation is intrastate-only and the state has adopted its own rule, that state rule controls.
